en: The Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the land where Tathāgatas roam, the Realm Adorned with Jewels.

The majestic site of enlightenment—this is entirely that which has been established by Perfect Awakening; it is adorned with great virtue and relies upon the accumulation of wondrous karmic deeds, being the fruition of Buddhahood. Within the palaces of the various Bodhisattvas, they proclaim the immeasurable transformations of the Tathāgatas; they enter bottomless wisdom and roam within a supreme mind filled with joy. They analyze and discern the universally equal holy practices cultivated, and they extol the boundless merits and infinite renown of the future Equal Perfect Awakenings. Having realized the Buddha-way, they skillfully turn the wheel of Dharma, transforming and enlightening countless disciples. Thus, they always attain mastery over all dharmas; knowing the nature of sentient beings and understanding their faculties, they ferry them to the other shore. Using timely expedient means, they remove all obstructions; their Buddha-activities dwell nowhere, yet they dwell in non-dwelling.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of six million bhikṣus—whose mental conduct was harmonious and peaceful, who had extinguished the afflictions of worldly toil, sensual attachment, and all manner of evils; who were the Dharma-princes of the Tathāgata, having cultivated profound dharmas born of the True Dharma; whose dignified deportment and ritual decorum were radiant in every movement, and who served as the refuge and protector for the great multitude, returning to the Tathāgata as their kin.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by an infinite number of bodhisattvas, so numerous as to be beyond measure. All were great sages who had attained mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), having acquired *dhāraṇī* and unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Their divine wisdom was so exquisitely profound that it could not be compared to anything. In a single moment of thought, they traveled to immeasurable lands to make offerings to the assemblies of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions. Clearly discerning what was to be honored, they listened to the Dharma without weariness, inquiring, receiving, and proclaiming it; they constantly maintained diligent cultivation and instructed the masses. Possessing universal skillful means and wisdom, their deliverance was boundless. They established the "Unobstructed Gate" (*anāvaraṇa-mukha*) and all transcended false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Being neither bound by response nor non-response, they drew near to the stage of all-encompassing knowledge and all-pervasive wisdom.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Celestial Radiance, Bodhisattva Chosen Battle, Bodhisattva Illuminating Treasury, Bodhisattva Removing Arrogance, Bodhisattva Valiant Stride, Bodhisattva Eye-Faculty, Bodhisattva Transcending Speech, and Bodhisattva Dispelling Darkness. Such as these were the members of the assembly of bodhisattvas; their vast, brilliant, and inconceivable virtues were all like this.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the practice for fulfilling the vows of all bodhisattvas; this dharma is called the Gate of the Unobstructed Canopy (*anāvaraṇa-mukha*). It purifies the sublime and wondrous sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all bodhisattvas; through the power of the True Awakening, it is endowed with fearlessness; it is the chamber of noble wisdom where one dwells among all dharmas and attains sovereignty; it encompasses the seals of *dhāraṇī* and brings clarity to eloquence; and by means of great supernormal powers, it universally reaches the illumination of the gates of the Way.

They eloquently expound and distinguish the wheel of non-retrogression and other teachings to guide those on the various vehicles; they penetrate the single dharma-realm without causing any disruption, proclaiming the faculties, intentions, and natures of sentient beings; they are adept at discerning the firm essentials and resolving all dharmas, thereby subduing the field of Māra.

In accordance with what is appropriate and in harmony with the Dharma, they are able to transform and enlighten those bound by the fetters of worldly toil, those deluded by false views, and those harboring the sixty-two doubts; they expound unimpeded wisdom, clearly understand the boundless, and immediately dispatch the karmic actions they have encouraged and assisted.

They enter the wisdom of the equal path of all Buddhas, a gateway of non-giving, non-expectation, and no fixed location; they expound all dharmas in accordance with the profound truth, treating equally those with perception and those without perception; they clearly understand the deep and subtle twelvefold dependent origination, accumulating merit and virtue beyond measure.

They adorn the bodily, verbal, and mental conduct of all Buddhas; their resolve is attained through the body, and their knowledge is inexhaustible. They cultivate the Four Noble Truths and instruct the śrāvakas in the tranquility of body and mind. They transform those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle so they may attain omniscience (sarvajñatā), and they possess the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) while promoting the study of the Mahāyāna. Entering into all dharmas with sovereign mastery, they walk alone, extolling the meritorious virtues of the Tathāgata.

He proclaims the teachings according to the occasion, comforting and sustaining them with tenderness; he instructs them gradually, elucidating the treasury of the Dharma to reveal its locus, and removing these subtle obscurations to manifest brilliant illumination.
The World-Honored One expounded and explained the Dharma teachings, causing them to spread far and wide throughout the ten directions.
At that time, a great golden light spontaneously appeared in the east; this light illuminated this Jewel-Pure Bodhimanda and shone upon the trichiliocosm, pervading everywhere without exception.

The brilliant and magnificent radiance of this Great Light completely eclipsed this land; the majestic splendors of the sun, the moon, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings were no longer visible. The light of the Mahābrahmās, the various sublime and towering devas, as well as that of the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, all ceased; even the light of all the bright moon-jewels, flame-light jewels, and great blazing torches was extinguished.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, possesses infinite great radiance; only the bodily brilliance of the bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) is clearly manifested, while all other existing lights are extinguished and do not appear.

This great trichiliocosm is vast, remote, secluded, and shrouded in darkness; although the radiance of the sun and moon is immense and their majestic power is sublime, they cannot reach it. Yet, that region is entirely illuminated by his brilliance, and his light is not obstructed by trees, walls, Mount Sumeru, the Snowy Mountains, the Black Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Iron Ring Mountains, or the Great Iron Ring Mountains.

That light passed through and illuminated the trichiliocosm, reaching from the Avīci Hell up to the highest reaches of the universe. Those dwelling among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals were all suffused by the radiance of this Way; their manifold sufferings were entirely eliminated, their afflictions and pains ceased, and their bodies and minds became peaceful. Each congratulated the others, each considering themselves to have encountered a fortunate time.

To the left of the Buddha, within the Pure Jewel Maṇḍala, sixty *koṭī-nayuta* lotus flowers made of the seven treasures spontaneously appeared. Their fragrance was so exquisite that it spread everywhere, bringing joy to all who smelled it;
the petals were soft and large as chariot wheels, their radiance brilliant and dazzling, with countless billions of leaves formed of hundreds of thousands of jewels, their shape perfectly round.

Upon these flowers were spread canopies of interlaced lattices adorned with pearl parasols; the sweet and exquisite fragrance emanating from these flowers pervaded the entire trichiliocosm. Consequently, all the renowned incenses possessed by the devas and humans throughout these three thousand realms vanished upon encountering this floral scent. Among all classes of beings dwelling in the heavens and the world, those who bore this flower fragrance all took delight in the fragrance of the Dharma and no longer relished sensual desires.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, beholding such a sign—an infinite radiance and a pure lotus flower—was filled with immeasurable wonder and joy. He immediately rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and asked the World-Honored One:
"What auspicious omen is this that you have now beheld, appearing in such a form, manifesting great radiance and an incalculable number of pure lotus flowers?"
"Since time immemorial, we have never seen or heard of such a thing.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There is a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati who has come from the eastern direction, accompanied by sixty billion bodhisattvas and surrounded by his retinue. Because he wishes to arrive in this land, he has first manifested these auspicious signs."

Not long after the Buddha had spoken, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati appeared at that moment, accompanied by six billion bodhisattvas. Then, through the infinite majestic power of a bodhisattva, he manifested great supernormal feats; the transformation of this *kai-shi* (bodhisattva) shook the Buddha-field, radiating a great brilliance and raining down various flowers and incense, while simultaneously performing hundreds of thousands of musical instruments.

Then, proceeding to the vast and universal Jewel-Purity Bodhimanda, he approached the Buddha’s presence and remained in the upper void as if standing upon the ground. With palms joined in self-surrender, he addressed the trichiliocosm with a single voice, praising the World-Honored One with verses of meaning:
“The Holy Hero has abandoned craving and desire; He is pure and free from defilement.
His wisdom dispels the profound darkness, Bestowing the eye of clarity.”
Having severed the three defilements of weariness and fatigue, And exhausted all manner of faults,
forever extinguishing all worldly afflictions, I now bow my head in homage to the Buddha.
He has cast away all that is broken and ruined, And transformed and rent asunder the net of ignorance.
The Holy Lord possesses the ten powers; he completely subdues all who fear.
Transcending the great assembly, having abandoned the three forms of negligence in tranquil solitude, he strides alone like a lion, moving through the world without fear.
That stainless radiance shines everywhere without exception;
universally mindful of all beings, it delivers them from every defilement.
For those obscured by ignorance and hidden in darkness, it eliminates all obstructions and gloom.
The radiance of his light shines forth like the sun emerging from the clouds.
Seeing the many people in solitary suffering, he gives rise to compassion;
he eliminates old age, sickness, and death, providing protection for those who have no savior.
The Guide entices sentient beings with vast compassion and constant pity;
his practiced deeds are like a physician treating all maladies.
The Honored One, Śāriputra, leads the assembly and transforms ignorance, folly, and stupidity.
Having heard of the afflictions of others, he delivers them like a ferryman;
he transforms countless defilements and the manifold delusive thoughts that arise.
In whatever place he dwells or travels, he remains unattached like a lotus flower.
Having realized that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and quiescent, one understands that the sounds uttered by the mouth all arise from causes and conditions.
What is without basis is produced through delusion; it is brought about by habitual practice.
Compassionate and filled with pity for the world, you bestow instruction upon all sentient beings.
We take refuge in you who are like space;
seeing all things as such, you abide within worldly dharmas yet remain unmoving like a great mountain.
Sentient beings, due to a lack of awakening, habitually practice unnecessary karma;
yet though they wander through their dwelling places, they shall all cross over the perils of birth and death.
The eye of the Way is exceedingly clear and bright, just like a blue lotus flower.
His majestic spiritual power is towering and sublime, like the fullness of the moon.
All people throughout the world together praise his virtue;
having abandoned affliction and no longer delighting in the mundane, they therefore bow their heads in homage to the Buddha.

Thereupon, Akṣayamati, together with six billion bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with these verses, descended from the void, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Sage seven times, and withdrew to sit upon lotus flowers.
Then Śāriputra, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, stepped forward and asked:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
From where has the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati come?"
What is the name of that Buddha?
What is the nature of his land?
How far away is that world from here, and by how much distance is it removed?
The Buddha said, "Ask Akṣayamati yourself; he shall provide you with an answer.
Then Śāriputra questioned Akṣayamati:
“O noble son! How far is the place from which you have come?
What is the name of that Buddha?”
"What is this world like?
Then Akṣayamati replied to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir, do you still maintain the notion of coming and going?"
Śāriputra said:
"Yes, son of noble family!
My conceptualizations have already been severed."
Akṣayamati said: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
One whose perceptions have been severed does not harbor duality in their will. For what reason would they give rise to a thought to ask such a question as 'from where do you come'?"
"Indeed, Śāriputra! That which comes is the trace of meeting;

if there were going, it would be the trace of parting. If one were to cause neither meeting nor parting, then there would be no coming or going. This absence of coming and going is the practice of the Noble Path."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!
That which comes is the mark of spontaneous arising; that which goes is the mark of the exhaustion of sin and merit.

To calculate sin and merit is to have the mark of spontaneity; if one exhausts all marks regarding sin and merit, then there is no mark. That which has no mark of going is the destination of the Noble Path."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

That which comes is called the characteristic of what is sought; that which goes is free from what is sought. The characteristic of what is sought being separated from the characteristic of where one goes is the characteristic of the Noble Path."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

That which comes has the characteristic of arising; that which goes has the characteristic of cessation. Apart from the characteristics of arising and going, that which neither arises nor ceases and does not go anywhere is the characteristic of the Noble Path."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

Those who come are for the sake of the gate of instruction; those who go are for the sake of teaching until all is exhausted. When one gives rise to the gate of neither instruction nor exhaustion, one then proceeds toward the Noble Path."
"O Śāriputra! If there is coming and going, one falls into the mundane; only when there is no going or coming can it be called the Way. O Śāriputra!"
By eliminating what has come and removing what is yet to come, as well as all objective realms, one proceeds toward the Noble Path.
"Venerable Śāriputra!

That which comes possesses the characteristic of the present; that which goes possesses the characteristic of departure. Upon reaching the characteristics of the present and of departing, one proceeds toward the Noble Path."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

That which comes is the mark of dependent origination as retribution; that which goes is the exhaustion of the marks of retribution. Where there is no retribution, there is neither arising nor ceasing; reaching the state of signlessness (animitta), one proceeds toward the Noble Path."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

Those who come do so by following the convergence of worldly conditions to reach the path; those who depart take sounds, verbal teachings, and written characters as their path. However, if one sets aside the paths of sound, writing, and causal conditions, one then proceeds toward the Noble Path."
Then Śāriputra asked Akṣayamati:
"O son of good family!
Because you possess such eloquence, I now wish to question you."
The reason for this is that one wishes to hear and examine what has not been heard before.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A gatekeeper in charge ought to interrogate those entering and exiting regarding their comings and goings; whether they carry valuable goods or travel empty-handed, because he wishes to collect taxes, he should appropriately challenge and question them.
"What have you brought that you would pay as tax at this time?
"Indeed, son of good family!
I am just like that."

Fools like us belong to the lineage of the śrāvakas; we attain liberation by relying on the voices of others and should constantly consult and receive instruction from those who correspond to conditions and echoes. You noble beings should protect and nurture this Great Vehicle, for from it are born the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, well done, son of good family!
Please explain in detail where you have come from, how far it is from here, and what the name of the Tathāgata’s land is called.
Aksayamati said: "Yes, Śāriputra!
You may now pose your questions to the Tathāgata who is present before us; he shall provide the answers, and the entire assembly will be graced by the resolution of their webs of doubt."
Then Śāriputra stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
"How far is it from here to the place where the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati has come from?
What is the name of that Buddha?"
"What is the nature of that land?
Those who hear its name, being incalculable in number, shall all resolve their minds upon the Way and don the great armor of virtue.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, listen attentively and reflect well.
That world is named Renowned for Merit, and as for the name of the Tathāgata therein, should anyone hear it, do not harbor doubts, but believe in it all together.”
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is without obstruction and free from the hindrances; he is all-pervasive in his wisdom and there is nothing he does not thoroughly understand.
They all replied, “We shall receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"To the east of here, passing beyond as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in ten Ganges rivers, and crossing over that many worlds, there is a world named Animiṣā. There dwells a Buddha named Samantabhadra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma. 'Animiṣā' means 'Unblinking' in the language of Jin;
'Samantabhadra' means 'Universal Virtue' in the language of Jin."

"In the world-system 'Unblinking,' there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; the World-Honored One’s holy assembly consists solely of bodhisattvas who have fully prepared their practices in past ages, practicing generosity and disciplining their minds, being composed and sagely, observing the precepts and possessing vast learning, being tranquil and free from negligence, and establishing themselves in contentment and quietude."
By the power of patience, his mind harbors no malice;
with firm diligence, he accumulates merit and virtue, constantly exercising self-restraint in every life, and universally enters the meditative absorptions of the gates of liberation and samādhi.

They delight themselves with the wisdom of supernormal powers, and through the radiance of the light of infinite knowledge, they discern according to the occasion and proclaim the meanings and principles of all chapters and phrases.
The compassion they harbor is equal to empty space; their pity is steadfast as they take pity upon sentient beings, knowing their dispositions and inclinations to transform and guide them.
Their joy rains down the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma, clearing away all anger, resentment, and knots of enmity.

Their practice of equanimity transcends the two vehicles, establishing the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, thereby rescuing others from the afflictions of worldly toil, the various māras, and the calamities of defilement and pollution.

Clearly understanding the fundamental tendencies of sentient beings through the twelve links of dependent origination, he observes their ailments and administers medicine accordingly; he governs this mind with constant equanimity, like earth, water, fire, and wind, free from both hatred and affection.

"He has cast off all various heterodox teachings and engaged in the battle of diverse dharmas, firmly planting his banner like a valiant general leading a great army who subdues a formidable enemy. He has entered the profound awakening of the True Dharma of all Buddhas, possessing the ten powers and fearlessness, remaining detached from the two extremes. He accords with the karma of existence and non-existence through causes and conditions, transcending all views and the intermediate states of practice. He has abandoned the notions of self, person, life-span, and the locus of existence or non-existence, turning back from the root of false views that oppose the truth."

"The gateways of all the sūtras are sealed with the Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma; the eloquence he expounds is without obstruction. Throughout incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, his vocal expressions cannot be hindered or blocked so as to prevent their free flow. By means of the Buddha’s supernormal powers, he transforms immeasurable Buddha-lands, circling back and forth, beginning again and again."
Fully understanding the appropriate timing, he eliminates all fear, anger, pride, and arrogance; the sound of his speech is like the roar of a lion and like the crashing of thunder.
He observes the superior, middling, and inferior conduct of sentient beings; as a steadfast friend, he establishes them forever in the ground of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

He raises infinite clouds, evokes the thunder of the Dharma, flashes the lightning of wisdom and liberation, and rains down the water of sweet dew. He proclaims the jewels of the Path and Dharma, ensuring the Three Jewels are never interrupted. His will and nature are pure like a bright moon-pearl; he is transparent both within and without, and his sublime marks and signs shine with the radiance of perfect enlightenment.

Thus, they adorn themselves with the prohibitive precepts and embellish their bodies with hundreds of thousands of virtues; they reverently practice in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas up to the stage of *avaivartika* and the state of being "born but once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*); they have profound faith in sentient beings, opening them to liberation and causing each to find their proper place according to their own dispositions and natures.

Taking the *dhāraṇī* of the awakened mind as his lion throne, he purifies the site of enlightenment; with clear discernment, he transcends and enters the four fearlessnesses, manifesting all the activities undertaken by the Buddhas and the noble body of perfect awakening, including its selections, relinquishments, advances, and retreats. His mind is powerful and courageous, attaining mastery as he turns the jewel of the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the assembly, hearing of the meritorious virtues of these bodhisattvas, was filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves; a clear mind arose within them. They then took exquisite celestial lotuses of blue, yellow, red, and white, as well as various mental flowers, and together offered them to the Buddha, scattering them over the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati and all the other bodhisattvas. With one voice, they raised their voices to extol his majestic virtue, saying:

"We have gained a great benefit and attained auspicious merit, for we have been able to encounter and meet such a Righteous Being (Samyaksambuddha-satpuruṣa). We prostrate ourselves, take refuge, and make offerings to him."

If there are sentient beings who hear the names of this assembly of bodhisattvas, their merit will be immeasurable; by virtue of what they have heard, they shall all give rise to the great bodhicitta.
At that time, all thirty-six thousand people who had gathered there resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“In the land of Animiṣā, there are no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor are there the various sufferings of evil states; there is neither the observance of precepts nor the transgression of prohibitions, and women are neither seen nor heard.”

Why is this? It is because they are all born by transformation within lotus flowers covered with dew; they possess no stinginess or greed, nor do they have lust or anger; they are free from delusion and fear. Since even the names of these three poisons are entirely absent there, how much more so for any others?

“The people of that land have no distinctions of superior, middling, or inferior, nor of beautiful or ugly; they are universally equal and without difference. Furthermore, they possess neither the notion of ‘I’ nor ‘what belongs to me,’ and they do not consume food or drink.”
Why is this so? Taking joy in the Dharma as food and understanding its meaning as drink, one is always naturally composed and never thinks of thirst, nor does one have any thought of hunger.
Furthermore, because there is neither self nor other, there is no affliction from the terrors and difficulties of the various Māras.
Moreover, that buddha-field is exceedingly vast; a single sun and moon illuminate sixty billion regions of the four quarters.
Why is this so? It is due to the power of the original vows of the bodhisattvas; for this reason, they share one sun and one moon.
Furthermore, that land has no mounds, ruins, elevations, depressions, or slopes; it is everywhere level and even, entirely composed of lapis lazuli, interspersed with various precious gems.
The ground is as soft as celestial silk, and the realm is adorned with eighteen kinds of excellences.

All the trees are made of jewels, arranged in orderly rows; they constantly produce flowers and fruit, remaining lush throughout both winter and summer, and are free from the defects of grit, pebbles, stones, or any impurities.
The Black Mountains, the Snowy Mountains, and all the mountains of that land are composed of a mixture of various jewels, just like Mount Sumeru.

In that buddha-field, the heavens and the world below are equal and without distinction; having abandoned worldly affairs, the land is governed by the Dharma, and there is no king other than the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, the Truly Realized One, who serves as the Dharma King.

Furthermore, according to the laws of that land, they do not instruct the bodhisattvas through written words; when they wish to consult and receive the sutras, they go to the Buddha’s abode, where they behold him without weariness and never grow weary.

Why is this? Because their minds were joyful, they immediately attained the meditative concentration of the Buddha-mind at that moment, and soon thereafter they drew near to the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
For this reason, that land is named "Unblinking" (Aparāmita).
What is meant by attaining the Buddha’s mind and meditative concentration?

It is not attained through physical marks, nor through the secondary characteristics, nor is it brought about by past habitual practices; nor is it sought after with the hope of achieving such a state.

Why is this? It is because one does not dwell upon the past or the future, nor does one dwell upon the present world; furthermore, it is not brought about by means of the five aggregates or the six sense-fields.
"What are the five?
The five aggregates refer to the six sense faculties; these six sense faculties refer to what is distinguished by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."

As for these six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one knows forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*) not through seeing, hearing, mind, intellect, or consciousness; this is brought about by the accumulation of various karmas, and is not brought about by the arising and ceasing of clever artifice or deception.

It is without equal and without deviation; it does not involve the formation of intention, nor is there anything hoped for. It is not brought about by "it is so" or "it is not so," nor is it brought about by one, two, or three.

It is not brought about by mind, thought, or consciousness; nor is it brought about by the understanding of internal or external matters, or by various thoughts and delusions, or by the affairs of right and wrong. Nor is it brought about by form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor is it brought about by the precepts, concentration, mindfulness, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the various dharmas of the Buddhas cannot be known through conceptual thought; they are brought about by that which transcends seeing and hearing.

One does not rely on the marks of perception, nor is there the notion of a self; one does not rely on the places of arising and ceasing of the five aggregates or the six sense-fields, nor is there any dwelling, nor is there any non-dwelling.

There is no locus for formlessness, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor is it brought about by the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, or the mind and dharmas; furthermore, no such locus can be found.
Why is this? It cannot be seen with the eyes as a collection of marks; it cannot be perceived in a place of thought, for that which is invisible cannot be seen.

It neither arises nor ceases; that which does not end has no beginning. This state of abiding is brought about by causes and conditions, leading to this very point: the elimination and return to extinction of the defilements of worldly toil.
Why is this so? Because of craving and desire, it is said that they must be extinguished.
For this reason, one cuts off causal conditions; because of the notion of "self," these too must be extinguished.
Their purity is entirely luminous, neither increasing nor decreasing, and they likewise do not conceive thoughts of this as peace or that as suffering.

Those who harbor such calculations are not free from desire; yet, they do not regard the absence of such thoughts as a vexation, for all perceptions are fundamentally liberated. Thus their practice is complete, and having attained such completeness, they realize the state of being without a self.
"If form cannot be apprehended, how can there be sensation?
How can there be perception?
Abiding eternally according to the Dharma, if one does not conceptualize the Path, then it is not worldly karma."
If there is nothing heard, from what could consciousness arise?

That which has nothing seen also has nothing attained; one who has nothing attained may be said to be liberated. Furthermore, one does not engage in mental reflection or universal contemplation regarding the dharmas that the mind perceives, nor does one maintain or grasp at anything unarisen.
One does not behold the coming nor see the rebirth; these are fundamentally unobtainable, for all phenomena are equal and without distinction.
It is like a person looking upward at the sky; what the eyes perceive cannot be distinguished as to what is space and what is not empty space.
The Buddha’s intention was thus:

when a bodhisattva attains the concentrated mind of a Buddha, they know all the Buddha-dharmas; they fully perfect the various marks and secondary characteristics; their wisdom of the Way becomes complete; and regarding all that the Tathāgata proclaims, they are able to understand and expound it for all bodhisattvas. Thereupon, they immediately receive, recite, and master it, becoming universally and thoroughly proficient in understanding all the Buddha-dharmas.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The Tathāgata Samantabhadra never utters two different words in what he proclaims.
What are these two? They are as follows:”
First, not to speak of attachment; second, not to speak of cessation.
To cultivate all things with equanimity, without partiality or bias.
What is meant by "non-existence"?

They never had the thought of seeking instruction from others, nor did they ever think that they themselves possessed any knowledge; as soon as these bodhisattvas beheld the Buddha, they immediately became fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
The Buddha said:
"How is it fulfilled?
By relinquishing all perceptions of form and having no expectations, this is the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)."
If one does not conceive of the Buddha-body and realizes its fundamental non-existence, then one has already fully perfected the *pāramitā* of precepts.
Why is this so? Because by not conceiving of a self, one achieves the accomplishment of the thirty-two marks.
One reckons that all dharmas are merely provisional designations; their marks are inexhaustible and abiding in non-arising. For this reason, it is called the Perfection of Patience (Kṣāntipāramitā).
All dharmas are universally invisible and likewise inaudible.

Why is this so? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not rejoice upon seeing good nor feel sorrow upon seeing evil; his mind is free from attachment or aversion. For this reason, it is called the Perfection of Vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
When the mind does not dwell upon that which is inconceivable, yet remains tranquil and serene, it is therefore called the Perfection of Tranquility (Dhyānapāramitā).
To understand that the characteristics of form are empty, and not to harbor arrogance on account of such characteristics, is therefore called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said:
"Those bodhisattvas who dwell in that land have, by means of this, fully perfected the six pāramitās and attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena."

Having universally examined the studies of the bodhisattvas in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there are few who can equal those bodhisattvas taught by Samantabhadra in the Akṣobhya realm.
Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"How wonderful, O worthy one!
The meritorious achievements of the multitude of bodhisattvas in that buddha-field are immeasurable."
Akṣayamati then asked Śāriputra:
"Venerable one, do you wish to see the land of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra in the realm of Animiṣā?
Śāriputra replied:
"I only wish to see him, so that all those gathered here may receive his grace and be blessed with increasing merit and virtue.

At that moment, Akṣayamati, while remaining seated, entered into a samādhi and manifested supernormal powers—a samādhi known as "Universally Beholding All Buddha-lands"—causing all those in the assembly, including Śāriputra, to behold the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra and the Buddha Animiṣa in their entirety. All were filled with joy at this unprecedented marvel and rose together to prostrate themselves before that Buddha in salutation.

By the holy intent of the Buddha, Śāriputra and those in the assembly each had celestial flowers and incense spontaneously appear upon their robes; they then took them and scattered them toward the east over that Buddha.
When those flowers reached that land, they rested above the Buddha’s head, pervading all the bodhisattvas throughout the entire buddha-field.
The bodhisattvas of that land asked their own Buddha:
“These flowers are now so subtle, exquisite, and extraordinary; from where have they come to possess such radiant splendor?”
The Tathāgata Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas:

"This auspicious omen signifies that Akṣayamati has now arrived in this Sahā world to serve and receive instruction from Śākyamuni Buddha; bodhisattvas from the ten directions have all gone to join him there."
"Why is this so? Because we expound the Mahāyāna.
The bodhisattvas of that land then asked the Buddha:
"What Buddha’s majestic spiritual power has brought about this manifestation of transformation here?
That Buddha replied,
"It is Śākyamuni Buddha."
Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all went to that assembly. Why was this?
Because they were expounding the Mahāyāna.
The bodhisattvas of that land again asked the Buddha,
"We have heard this here.
That Buddha replied:
"In the 'Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of the Great Assembly' from the *Sūtra of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s Extensive Exposition and Analysis,' that bodhisattva again questioned his Buddha:
'How far is that world of endurance (Sahā-lokadhātu) from here?'"
The Buddha said:

"To the west of here, as many buddha-lands as there are atoms of dust filling ten Ganges-sands of worlds, suppose one were to take a single atom and place it in one buddha-land; continuing in this manner until all those atoms have been taken and distributed sequentially throughout the buddha-worlds of the west, and having exhausted all those atoms, one would pass through that many lands until reaching the realm of endurance (Sahā), the dwelling and teaching site of Śākyamuni Buddha."
The bodhisattvas of that land again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only wish to behold the Great Sage Śākyamuni and the flourishing of his transformative teachings.
Thereupon, the Buddha Samantabhadra emitted a radiance from his body that illuminated the ten directions, so that all those bodhisattvas and the members of the assembly beheld this land.
Those bodhisattvas immediately all rose and, from afar, took refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha, bowing with single-minded devotion.
Seeing from afar that the Sahā world was filled with bodhisattvas, leaving no empty space, they were struck with wonder and joy, and questioned their own Buddha.
That Buddha told him:

"The multitudes of bodhisattvas from the buddha-lands of the ten directions are beyond measure; having heard that the 'Chapter on the Conditions for the Great Assembly' shall be proclaimed, they have come to receive its instruction."
Śāriputra asked the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"By whom was the name 'Akṣayamati'—which in the Jin language means 'Inexhaustible Intention'—given to you, O Venerable One?"
He replied:
“Śāriputra, it is because of all dharmas that they are said to be inexhaustible.”
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are likewise inexhaustible.
Śāriputra said:
"I pray that you explain this by means of the inexhaustible Dharma.
Akṣayamati said,
"The original generation of the aspiration [for enlightenment] is likewise inexhaustible."
Why is this so? Because although they are completely immersed in all desires and intoxicated by lust, anger, and delusion, they remain unbound. Why is this so?
Because they do not associate with the same defilements as those of the Arhat or Pratyekabuddha vehicles,
from the moment they first resolve their minds, they make their will firm and unshakable. Why is this so?
They are not deluded or misled by evil deeds, and no demons whatsoever can destroy their resolve.
One who possesses such a mind will fully accomplish all merits and virtues; though wandering amidst impermanence, they alone preside as the sovereign leader of the multitude.
Why is this so? Those who reckon things as permanent are subject to the karma of birth and death; therefore, one who especially honors and understands the Way as being eternal is called "Venerable.
Because they have transcended impermanence, from the moment they first resolve their mind, their heart remains serene and free from all fetters and attachments.
Why is this? Because they do not depart from the meritorious deeds of all Buddhas.
The undertakings they cultivate cannot be brought to failure; for this reason, all evils are completely exhausted, and their minds are eternally peaceful and immovable.
That mind has no peer; the reason for this is that it is rare to attain.
That mind is like a vajra; the reason for this is that it knows all dharmas and is therefore inexhaustible, as it encompasses the path-wisdom of all dharmas.

From the moment of generating the resolve, it has been as firm as a vajra; because it regards all sentient beings with equality, its mind is upright and free from flattery or deceit, and is thus called "correct" and without partiality.

"From the moment they first resolve their minds, they always maintain a state of clarity. This is because they are fundamentally pure; having removed all defilements and extinguished all darkness, their wisdom shines forth, illuminating even the most profound and hidden realms."
From the moment they first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they have bathed away all defilements; this is because their faith is exceedingly firm and they have nothing to relinquish.
Their resolve is vast and boundless, for their mind is like empty space.
The arousal of the mind is vast and open; the reason for this is that it embraces all sentient beings as they are to be delivered through the means of salvation.
The arousal of the mind is inexhaustible; the reason for this is that its wisdom is profound and expansive, free from all obstructions.
"From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, there is nothing they do not enter; this is because their great compassion is boundless and inexhaustible.
Their practice of generating that mind cannot be severed, for it is sustained by their merit and vows."
The arousal of the mind is profoundly peaceful and most worthy of veneration; for what reason? Because it is that which all sentient beings delight in.
This arousal of the mind is exceptionally honored and transcends all others; for what reason? Because it is that which all those of external paths, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas revere.
The intent of his resolve cannot be known by others, for it is not within the reach of ordinary people; it is just as a common farmer cannot understand or fathom the affairs of a sage-king.
One gives rise to a mind of its own kind; the reason for this is that each obtains its fruit according to its respective fundamental karmic seeds, for all phenomena (dharmas) exist eternally.
"Taking the initial aspiration for enlightenment as the foundation of the Way—why is this so? Because it is by means of this that one attains great peace.
From the moment the aspiration is first conceived, one adorns oneself—why is this so? Because it is through this that one achieves meritorious accomplishment."
Since first resolving their minds, they have been distinct from the masses; the reason for this is that they have attained noble wisdom.
Since first resolving their minds, they have been exceedingly subtle and wondrous; the reason for this is that they employ extensive giving to reach all sentient beings.
Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, they have established their ultimate vows; the reason for this is that they are fully endowed with the precepts and prohibitions.
Since first generating the aspiration, they have had no equal; the reason for this is that there is nothing they cannot endure.
Since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, it has been impossible to suppress it; this is because one practices with diligence and never allows for negligence or desistance.
Since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, there has been nothing to crave or delight in; this is because one has attained the concentration of the perfection of tranquility (*śamatha*).
Since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, they have no place of destination, because they have thoroughly understood the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, they never abide anywhere; this is because they employ immeasurable loving-kindness (maitrī).
Since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, their root and trunk have become firm and strong; this is because they practice compassion.
Since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, they have constantly harbored joy; this is because they maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Since generating this mind, although they encounter suffering or joy, they remain unmoved; the reason for this is that they protect all beings.
Since generating this mind, they have been looked upon and nurtured by all Tathāgatas; the reason for this is that they act in accordance with the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, they have sought to deliver all beings from the hardships of the five destinies; the reason for this is that they promote and flourish the guidance and transformation of others.

Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, they do not abandon the Three Jewels nor violate or neglect them; the reason for this is that they comply with the Buddha’s precepts in order to bring the assembly of noble ones to fulfillment.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati again addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Can the mind of omniscience ever be exhausted?
Śāriputra replied:
"No. Just as space cannot be exhausted, so too the mind of omniscience is likewise inexhaustible;
the Tathāgata’s precepts are also inexhaustible."
Why is this? Because morality is the root and source, it is inexhaustible.
The Tathāgata’s concentration of mind is likewise inexhaustible; his wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are inexhaustible because they have no root.
As for the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are the faculties; since these are also the fundamental nature of the mind, they are inexhaustible.
To state the essentials: all the teachings of the Buddhas take this as their primary principle; because one acts according to this mind, it is inexhaustible.
The Three Jewels are uninterrupted; because they arise from this mind, they are inexhaustible.
"It is just as the four great elements of all sentient beings—what are the four?
Earth, water, fire, and wind—which are likewise inexhaustible."
Because this wisdom functions for the sake of all, it thoroughly understands the inconceivable mental activities of sentient beings; because its original vows are uninterrupted, it is inexhaustible.

Why is this so? Because the vows for practicing and upholding the Way are inexhaustible; all things are non-arising and nothing is not ethereal and mysterious. Since the fundamental source of all dharmas is infinite, they are therefore inexhaustible.
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra: "The arousal of the bodhicitta is forever inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because it is not adorned with literary artifice, nor is it characterized by flattery."
His mind is upright and honest; thus it is called extraordinary. He does not employ flowery rhetoric because he is pure;

he is level and correct, free from depravity. His mind is supple and without coarseness; he has firm faith in the true essence that never alters. What he establishes is steadfast and immovable; dwelling correctly without wavering, no one can harbor hatred or jealousy to afflict or harm him.
For what reason is there no one able to disturb them?
Because their practice, governance, and karma are such that none can surpass them.
Whatever they establish, none are able to disparage.
Why is it that no one is able to censure or revile him?
It is because whatever he undertakes has no root or source. Why does it have no root?
Because it is based on the correct and the mean (the Middle Way).

What he says with utmost sincerity never differs from the truth; whatever meritorious deeds he undertakes, he harbors no expectations and seeks no fame. He is praised by all and held in universal veneration, such that none are able to find fault in him.
The reason no one is able to find fault with him is that he has cultivated long-standing peace and tranquility.
Why does he attain this eternal peace and tranquility for himself?
It is because the merit he generates is never weary or indolent, and it is because he never tires of showing compassion for all sentient beings.
Why is it that one takes pity on sentient beings?
It is because one employs infinite compassion to arouse diligence for those who are weary. Why is this so?
It is for the purpose of nourishing and raising sentient beings.
Why is it that they nourish and raise sentient beings?
It is because by means of this, they bring about the accomplishment of merit and virtue.
The power of what is cultivated does not hope for blessings; because there is no seeking, and because the mind is pure, one receives the grace of the Dharma and thus has nothing to seek.
Humans also possess power—what is meant by "power"?
It is said: This is the power of the Buddha, for by this principle he protects all beings;
the reason he protects them is that he desires to cause the multitudes to each attain their proper place;
the reason he desires to cause them to each attain their proper place is to ensure they have no regrets.
Thus there is no resentment, because the deeds one performs are extremely peaceful and certain;
they are certain because, for this reason, nothing can obstruct them, nor can anything admonish or suppress them so as to cause them to cease and become still.
It is like purple-gold that is free from any stain; it is likened to the color of purple-gold because it possesses no defilement.
It is without defilement because it is fundamentally pure;
it is pure because its original practice has removed all impurities.
"It is for the purpose of removing defilement, because the interior is thereby purified;
it is for the purpose of eliminating blemishes, because once the blemishes are exhausted, one becomes pure through this.
Acchamata said to Śāriputra:
"When the mind has become pure, craving and desire are further diminished; that which is free from craving and desire is inexhaustible.
Various evil thoughts can no longer disturb it, and furthermore, the mind is luminously protected against malevolent intentions; for this reason, it is called 'inexhaustible.'"

If that mind is prone to anger and various cravings, if it is busily preoccupied with desire, arrogant and conceited, and exhausts itself in all manner of what is improper—then a bodhisattva shall constantly guard this mind.

One should understand that this mind is inexhaustible; one should abandon its lack of vision, its power, and all its defilements. One should penetrate this mind so as not to allow indolence, thereby knowing that the mind is indeed inexhaustible.

If there are those who are agitated, he protects them according to the occasion; for those who lack wisdom, he nurtures and raises them until they are perfected. Calculating the factions of all sentient beings—whether they possess the dharmas of merit or lack the dharmas of merit—he delivers them all to great peace. Thus one knows that his mind is inexhaustible.
In instructing and admonishing all sentient beings alike, causing those who are in distress and difficulty to all establish boundless merit, one thereby knows that this mind can never be exhausted.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
“The practices cultivated by a bodhisattva are likewise inexhaustible. Why is this? Because—”
Because that which is given in charity is inexhaustible, all that can be bestowed is called the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*);
taking only what is sufficient from all things without being anxious or greedy is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*);
when all manner of afflictions assail the body of a bodhisattva, not giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of anger is called the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
That the merit one has accumulated always remains at the forefront of the assembly and never lags behind is called the practice of the perfection of vigor;
that one applies diligent effort to all that is studied is called the practice of the perfection of tranquility;
and that one desires to achieve comprehensive mastery of everything heard is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva should train in and cultivate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
What is meant by great loving-kindness?

If someone comes seeking refuge during times of distress and calamity, wishing to be saved and relieved, one would rather lose one's own body and life than fail to fulfill one's solemn vow; this is the practice of loving-kindness.

The practice of compassion is like a scale: whether one receives benefit, they do not feel joy; even if they are slandered, they do not feel sorrow. This is the bodhisattva’s impartial compassion according to the occasion.

"The training of a bodhisattva consists in purifying body, speech, and mind through these three matters; they never transmit evil, nor do they ever conceive thoughts of perverse, foolish, or deluded actions."

Although the bodhisattva trains in solitary progress without a teacher, he does not become conceited; his intent in training does not abandon universal wisdom, and through his various supernormal powers and swift intelligence, he grasps all the Buddha-dharmas and the deeds of a bodhisattva.
In all that people seek, he does not oppose their wishes; he leaves them without deficiency or lack, bringing forth all dharmas so that they attain mastery.
Furthermore, he practices repentance, never concealing any evils or transgressions of his body, and employs immeasurable merit to encourage and assist in the accumulation of virtue.

The Bodhisattva practices and trains in praising and exhorting all Buddhas to proclaim the meaning of the Way, and respectfully studies and diligently learns the Dharma of the true sages (*saddharmasatpuruṣa*);
the reason for studying this Dharma of the true sages is the desire to achieve enlightenment.
His mind is firm and resolute; he does not abandon the armor of infinite virtue consisting of his great vows. The reason he does not abandon them is that he desires to transform all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
"There are four things for which a bodhisattva is inexhaustible."
What are these four?
First is the mind of revelation; second is the gift of Dharma; third is the instruction of sentient beings; and fourth is the accumulation of merit.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four:
first, to habitually dwell in seclusion, living alone in mountain caves, accepting whatever alms are given with simple sufficiency;
second, to never feel satiety regarding the various meritorious virtues."
The third is to study extensively without weariness;
the fourth is not to regard the wisdom one seeks as laborious—
these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four:
first, calculating and planning; second, contemplating the beginning and the end; third, the thorough penetration of wisdom and discernment; fourth, the universal fulfillment of what is contemplated.
These are the four."
"Furthermore, there are four:

first, to distance oneself from all evils and cultivate supreme liberation; second, that this supreme liberation is the teaching of the Bodhisattva; third, to understand the root of all evils; fourth, to contemplate the subtle and unsurpassed liberation.
These are the four."
"Furthermore, there are four matters:

first, understanding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); second, comprehending the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind; third, realizing the source of the six sense-decays (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); and fourth, perceiving that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) have no limit.
These are the four."
"Furthermore, there are four matters:

first, the discourse on impermanence and the cycle of birth and death, which is inexhaustible; second, the teaching on suffering and pain; third, the instruction on non-self; and fourth, the practice of tranquility and non-action, which is also inexhaustible.
These are the four."
Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
“To state it briefly, all the trainings of bodhisattvas are proximate to the Buddha-way.
For this reason, the distinctions between the monastic and the lay are inexhaustible.”
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
"The mental cultivation of a bodhisattva is inexhaustible. Why is this so?"
They do not grow weary in the cultivation of all meritorious virtues, but progressively advance to achieve their respective stages;
what are called these "stages" are the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattva.
Their practice is like the great ocean, which encompasses all without satiety, for it is by means of this that they extensively deliver all sentient beings.

That which is practiced constitutes the foremost; the reason for this is that it emerges above all else. It is the supreme practice that can encompass everything, causing all those below to cultivate focused application in all dharmas, as if upholding a multitude of virtues.
Why is this? Because it is the most honored.
The reason one practices the liberations and thereby receives the prediction of enlightenment is entirely due to single-minded diligence.
Because one does not regress, one attains fulfillment; because of one's single-minded diligence, whatever is wished for is immediately accomplished, thereby fulfilling great vows.

That which is practiced without ever relying on anything else is the concentrated mind (*samādhi*); by relying on the cultivation of gentleness, the practitioner’s deeds remain without deficiency or leakage. Cultivating the subduing of the mind is the work of the Way (*mārga-karman*), and practicing self-restraint is the practice of guarding oneself.
Why is this? Because he no longer associates with various evils.
Through his single-minded dedication to giving, the Bodhisattva harbors no greed or attachment regarding body or mind, as these qualities continue to increase further.
To be single-mindedly devoted to upholding the precepts is also extremely difficult; the reason for this is that it involves teaching those who violate the precepts not to commit evil.

To be single-mindedly devoted to practicing patience is also extremely difficult; the reason for this is that even when one holds a position of honor, possesses great wealth, or enjoys supreme pleasure, one does not look down upon the poor, the lowly, the frail, or the weak—this is what constitutes patience.
The practice he cultivates is exclusively one of diligence that is difficult to equal. When he sits beneath the Bodhi tree, if someone were to come and say:
"Arise and move away; I shall sit in this place and first attain the Way of the Buddha."
To immediately relinquish one's dwelling place is what constitutes diligence.

As for the difficulty of single-minded meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-cintā*), it is that nothing can surpass it; whatever one cultivates with such single-mindedness is invariably accomplished because there is no expectation of reward—this is called meditative contemplation.
It is difficult to specialize in wisdom. Why is this?
To accumulate merit and cultivate virtue without being weary or fatigued—this is what constitutes wisdom.
“His coming and going and every step are calm, composed, and elegant; his majestic deportment is complete in every detail. This is because his merit and power are so great that none can harm him.
He cultivates the fearlessnesses, understands the profound Dharma, and grasps the subtle mysteries to reach the far-reaching.”
One should cultivate the mind of reverence; for what reason? Because its brilliance is so subtle and refined that there is nothing it does not penetrate.
Thus, its practice can never be exhausted. Why is this so?
The dwelling is firm and stable. What is meant by "single-minded application"?

It is when one’s mind is serene and constantly mindful of all beings: causing those who have no support to find support; causing those in darkness to behold the light of the Path; providing refuge for all who have no refuge; acting as a kind and generous friend to those who lack virtuous friends; causing the flatterers to cultivate sincerity and simplicity; and, upon seeing those who are coarse and fierce, manifesting patience, gentleness, and harmonious refinement.
Why is this? It is because they transform others through virtue. Amidst guile and deception, they reveal the true meaning; amidst ornamentation, they do not indulge in the grandiose;

amidst lack of reciprocity, they practice the repayment of kindness; amidst the presence of many evils, they cultivate wholesome conduct; amidst decline and neglect, they reverently cultivate merit; amidst deceit and arrogance, they always act with respect and diligence; amidst pride and conceit, they harbor no self-importance; amidst those seeking advantage, they find no fault; they do not dwell on the evil of others nor proclaim their deficiencies; and if they encounter those who are unrighteous, they immediately go to protect them and lead them into the truth of the Right Dharma.

"All sentient beings who come to this place see him with joy and without a mind of anger. Should there be those who offer admonitions or guidance regarding what is appropriate or inappropriate, what should be done or should not be done, his mind remains without increase or decrease; he firmly believes that the fruits of fortune and calamity resulting from one's actions return to oneself."

"If one dwells in the wilderness, in the mountains, or in rocky caves, acting in accordance with the Dharma without deviation, neither coveting gain or loss nor begrudging body or life, then because the mind is pure, it will from the outset neither increase nor decrease."
He constantly guards his speech and does not forget to refrain from spreading rumors, nor does he seek honor or respect. Why is this?
Because he always knows moderation and is content with what he has.
His mind is gentle and supple; because he possesses merit, he does not follow those who are corrupt, evil, or devoid of propriety and righteousness.
He transcends birth and death and brings rest to all suffering and affliction.

Why is this so? For this reason, the wisdom-mind of a bodhisattva is forever inexhaustible, and their traversing through birth and death is likewise inexhaustible. Through clear understanding of skillful means, they instruct sentient beings who are deluded regarding the beginning and end of existence—beings who are themselves inexhaustible—causing them to seek the Buddha-way, which is also clearly seen to be inexhaustible.
Śāriputra asked Akṣayamati,
“Are there other things that are inexhaustible?
Akṣayamati replied:
“There is. He asked: “What is it?”
Akṣayamati said:
“The giving of a bodhisattva is likewise inexhaustible. Why is this? Because—”
Because the six perfections are inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s giving is entirely without limit.
What is meant by "limit" is as follows:

to think that "this person is right and that person is wrong," or "I should give to such-and-such a person but not to such-and-such another"; to give without universal relief, or to give in a manner that is not true giving.
Śāriputra asked,
"How should the Dharma of a bodhisattva be practiced in giving?
Akṣayamati replied:
"The hungry shall eat it. Why is this?

It is because people depend upon food and clothing to sustain their lives; thus they are able to recover, sit up, and speak, thereby attaining peace and security, with their bodies healthy and their strength robust."
To those who are thirsty, one gives drink to eliminate their parching thirst. Why is this?
Because if they are in future lives, as they wander through birth and death, they will never again suffer from thirst or exhaustion.

Whenever anyone requested a vehicle, he would grant it according to their wishes; as a result of this merit, in all future births, he possesses the supernormal power of flight, reaching wherever he intends to go.
To those who lacked clothing, he gave them garments; consequently, in his subsequent lives, he is never coarse or aggressive, but always maintains a sense of shame and remorse.
If one offers lamps in dark places, one will attain the eye of the Way and see clearly throughout the ten directions.

If one provides music and entertainment before the World-Honored One, teachers, monasteries, parents, or elders, in future lives one will be born with the faculty of hearing that penetrates and hears all things infinitely.

If there is no fragrance, one should bestow it upon them; in future lives, they shall attain the fragrance of the precepts, wisdom, concentration, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, so that this body is perfumed by the scent of these virtues.
Furthermore, if there are those who seek various fragrances, he gives them whatever they desire; consequently, in future lives, his body will be so pure and fragrant that all will be delighted.

If there are people who come seeking sweet and extraordinary flavors, he immediately grants them according to their wishes; consequently, in future lives, he will always obtain delicacies, such that even what is not naturally savory becomes delicious as soon as it enters the mouth—this mark is obtained through what was planted in previous lives.
To those who lacked hand-towels, he gave them; in future lives, they will be born pure and stainless, protected by others.
For those who have no protector, he acts as their guardian, just like a house, for a house is used as a metaphor because it covers and shelters people.
According to what each lacks, one bestows gifts upon them; thus, in future lives, they shall all obtain what they deserve and immediately receive full provision.

By giving medicine to the sick, in future lives their bodies will always be free from illness, neither born nor dying, devoid of all afflictions, and constantly attaining peace and security; everything will be fully provided for, and there will be nothing they do not master.
He who lacks servants or attendants will, in future lives, naturally possess them;

he who is a sovereign of ten thousand chariots, governing superiors and subordinates, shall lack for nothing; he who seeks various treasures shall be able to provide them; and in future lives, he shall be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
By giving various kinds of miscellaneous items as alms, one will obtain the eighty minor marks of physical excellence in future births.
By giving elephants and horses, one will later attain the supreme intention of the Mahāyāna;
by giving fields, one will, through that cause, achieve the perfection of *śīla* (ethical discipline).
If one gives away one's wife and children, bestowing what is most cherished and beloved, and remains free from ulterior motives thereafter, one shall attain the Way of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because the Buddha is the supreme being, honored beyond compare.

"Suppose there were someone who, from that bodhisattva, requested a full granary of grain; he would immediately give it to them without ever being greedy or stingy. Later, having attained the treasury of the Dharma, his fulfillment of the wisdom of the Path will be such that nothing shall be lacking."

If a bodhisattva should become a wheel-turning monarch ruling over the four continents with the seven treasures in full abundance, and should there be those who come to him seeking anything, he would not cherish it but would immediately bestow it all as a gift; thereafter, in his future births, he shall attain omniscience and, through his various supernormal powers and noble wisdom, extensively deliver all beings.
Those who bestow exquisite music and performances will later obtain the sutras and delight in the joy of the Dharma, finding nothing but joy.

If, for the sake of power and status, one has loyal aides who practice the Bodhisattva path—just like the loyal ministers of a king—and when someone comes seeking their assistance in governing, one can grant it to them; by virtue of this, when the teachings of the Buddha later desire to sit at the site of enlightenment, one shall subdue the demonic armies beneath the Bodhi tree.
"By giving one's hands to others, one will later become the foremost among all paths and dharmas;
by giving one's ears and nose, one's body will later be fully endowed without a single deficiency;
by giving one's eyes, one will later attain the Dharma-eye, becoming the foremost eye of the path and dharmas for all."
By giving one's head as an offering, one will be uniquely honored in all three periods of time in future births, walking alone without peer, endowed with all supernormal powers and swift wisdom;
by giving flesh and muscle as an offering, one will later attain the Way of the Buddha and people will come to hear his preaching of the sutras;
by relinquishing all that is unnecessary, one obtains what is truly authentic.
"When a Bodhisattva breaks his own bones to give away his marrow, he shall later attain the Way of the Buddha, and his body will be like a vajra, incapable of being shaken.
Akṣayamati said, "A Bodhisattva does not practice giving for the sake of physical form; rather, he does so in order to cultivate correct practice."
If some come seeking much while others seek little, he gives to all equally so that each may be satisfied.
When giving, he is not afraid, terrified, fearful, or anxious; he practices generosity without greed, harbors no regret, and his mind never wavers.
A bodhisattva gives without contempt or arrogance, bestowing gifts with single-minded devotion;
they give without flattery or deceit, never offering inferior items or things that are worthless to others.

When a bodhisattva practices giving, they never examine whether someone possesses merit or another incurs transgression; free from doubt and making no distinction between the beautiful and the ugly, they do not interrupt or omit their practice of generosity.
What is meant by "giving that is interrupted or omitted"?
It is when, amidst a great assembly, one gives to only a single person and not to another, despite desiring to provide universal relief to all. Why is this so?
The bodhisattva’s giving is always characterized by profound faith; he does not harbor thoughts of weariness or fatigue, nor does he give with a mind of affliction or distress.

When a bodhisattva practices giving, he does not call people forward, but only bestows gifts upon those whose faces he beholds with his own eyes. Furthermore, he does not contemplate whether someone is good or evil, nor does he select recipients specifically for those who have attained the Way; rather, he gives to whoever comes before him.
After giving to others, one does not form such thoughts as:
"So-and-so has attained the Way; so-and-so has not attained the Way.

When a Bodhisattva practices giving, he is not delighted to see a person who upholds the precepts come to receive his gift, nor does he harbor any different feelings toward one who lacks the precepts. His giving is free from expectation of recompense; regarding that which he bestows, he seeks no fame for it to be heard far and wide, nor does he praise himself or disparage others.
“A Bodhisattva gives without causing disturbance, without harboring resentment while giving, without anger while giving, and without lack of joy while giving.

When a Bodhisattva practices generosity, they do not think of obtaining merit in future lives; they do not give with a mind of malice or by reviling the foolishness of their gift. When someone comes to seek something, they do not push them away before giving it to them; they do not give with contempt, nor do they entrust others to carry the objects to the recipient.”
Why is this? Because he personally pours the wine with his own hands,
nor does he even think to say:
"When one encounters me, one should give; those who do not encounter me should not give to them.
One gives without obstruction, giving with a mind of one's own accord;
one does not give with haste or violence, but bestows it with one's own hands.
He does not give with hesitation, alternating between giving and not giving.
The Bodhisattva does not think:
"The act of giving causes me exhaustion and extreme fatigue."
In giving to those who come, he gives neither too much nor too little; he does not discriminate between objects, giving what is inferior and keeping what is superior.
If there is one who comes seeking, he fulfills his original promise without ever diminishing it.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they take pity on sentient beings and act with great impartiality, desiring that the recipients always obtain peace and security.
When bestowing a gift, they think:
"This person belongs to my realm."
Why is this? Because everything is the ground of the Bodhisattva’s path.
Furthermore, regarding what is given, one does not disparage oneself when it is little, nor does one rejoice excessively when it is much.
Although he gives much, he does not examine himself by saying,
"I am now giving extensively and bestowing according to the Dharma," because he has no expectation of reward.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they do not think:
"This merit shall give rise to a place of rebirth where I may receive its karmic reward. Why is this?
Because all sentient beings receive his grace through his giving,
the donor does not think:
"I alone have attained supreme power among those in heaven, those on earth, and those among humans."

Whatever they give is universally for the sake of all sentient beings; they do not seek or long for the positions of the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, or Brahmā through that merit, nor do they covet the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, nor do they cultivate the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, his mind does not harbor the thought,
"My giving is complete," nor does he contemplate whether it is meager, sufficient, or insufficient.
As for those who practice giving, they cause all sentient beings not to be separated from the Buddha’s various supernormal powers and swift wisdom;
as for those who bestow gifts, they always act at the appropriate time, with nothing that is unsuitable.
He does not bestow weapons or poisons;
he bestows peace upon others and inflicts no harm.

The bodhisattva’s giving follows the teachings of the Buddha: he knows that all things bestowed are empty. Yet, because the act of giving serves as a causal condition for the arising of wholesome qualities, it is therefore inexhaustible.

Those who practice giving fully understand the absence of conceptualization (*animitta*); because they establish the causal conditions for all those with conceptualizations, this giving is inexhaustible.

Those who practice giving all realize the absence of aspiration (*apraṇihita*); because they create virtuous causal conditions for all those with aspirations, by virtue of this appropriateness, it is inexhaustible.
When one practices giving with the intention of the Dharma, the mind becomes firm and strong, fully perfected and profoundly peaceful, remaining indestructible.

Whatever a Bodhisattva gives within the triple world cannot be equaled by any other; in whatever they bestow, they desire that its merit flow back to the deeds of all Bodhisattvas. Because their resolve is always established in the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), for this reason, it is inexhaustible.
That which is bestowed is inexhaustible because it liberates one from all conceptualizations, brings all Māras under control so they lack autonomy, and is free from all vexations and oppressions.
The giving of the Bodhisattva is uniquely transcendent; because it illuminates *nirvāṇa*, that which is bestowed decisively resolves the doubts of the multitude, and is therefore inexhaustible.
The giver dwells correctly in the Buddha-way without harboring divergent thoughts; because their giving is equal to their vows, it is inexhaustible.

The Bodhisattva’s giving results in attaining perfect enlightenment while seated beneath the Bodhi tree; because those who receive the gift and the countless, incalculable classes of sentient beings are all sustained and delivered, it is inexhaustible.

That which is bestowed can never be exhausted; its scope is vast and great. That which is bestowed attains the state of the Way, wherein nothing can move it and nothing can surpass it—how much more so the one who bestows it?
Therefore, it is inexhaustible.
The mind of one who practices giving is serene and expansive, like that of the All-Knowing One;
thus, it is inexhaustible. Śāriputra said:
“Excellent, excellent!
O worthy one, Akṣayamati, it is truly marvelous that you have praised the inexhaustibility of the bodhisattva’s giving. How wonderful this is!
We wish to receive and hear the meaning of the inexhaustible precepts and prohibitions of the bodhisattvas.”
Aksayamati said:
"The purity of the Bodhisattva precepts is likewise inexhaustible, consisting of sixty-four matters.
What are these sixty-four? "
The Bodhisattva practices benevolence and harbors no intent to harm toward sentient beings; he neither kills, nor takes the property of others, nor violates the wives of others.

When he encounters other Bodhisattvas or ordinary beings, he always acts with sincerity and never engages in double-tongued speech; when there are disputes, he constantly seeks to reconcile them, and never utters abuse or engages in harsh speech.
Why is this? Because they always possess a sense of shame and modesty; they guard their speech and do not speak falsely about matters.
Toward all people, they harbor no thoughts of envy, nor do they give rise to anger toward sentient beings.
Why is this? Because through this ability to endure, one will be handsome and upright in future lives;
one constantly rectifies the mind and does not pursue other studies, always maintaining a joyful heart within the Buddha-way.

Why is this? Because their minds are pure and free from defilement, and they delight in the Buddha-dharma. This is because they understand that there is no other dharma superior to this, and they abide wholeheartedly in the Way through the practice of loving-kindness and benevolence.
“Whenever one sees a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, one should immediately take refuge in them and pay homage with the five limbs.
What are these five?
They are the two hands, the two knees, and the head—bowing the crown of the head to their feet.”
Why is this? It is because, by attaining the Way of the Buddha, all beings take refuge in him.

His mind is always supple; when he sees others committing transgressions, he is careful of himself and does not do likewise. He is never deficient in his precepts, for he possesses no mind of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
