Regarding those who violate the precepts, he commits no offense. Why is this?
Because he does not desire to be reborn in future lives among hunters, fishermen, or families of ignorance and darkness.
He constantly cultivates diligence and is never indolent. Why is this?
Because he does not associate with or follow after evil, his observance of the precepts is complete and never lacking.
Because they associate with those of wisdom and virtue who understand the profound Dharma, they do not oppose or distance themselves from them;
because they have sincere faith in the prohibitions and precepts, that which they uphold is correct;
and because they accord with the precepts according to the Dharma, all sentient beings sing their praises.
Their protection of the precepts is pure and reaches the ultimate truth because their fundamental mind is joyful;
they practice the essentials of the precepts so that no one can transmit false teachings or speak of their flaws, for they have no deviant mind;
their precepts are complete and perfect, and they are no longer deluded by the six sense-decadences.
The precepts one upholds are renowned far and wide, for they are known by all the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones;
the precepts involve no seeking, for they are as joyful as one’s own self;
the precepts consist in knowing contentment, for there is nothing craved.
Their precepts are pure and refined, unmixed with various evils, for their bodies and minds are serene and have nothing to delight in;
they always prefer dwelling in seclusion, never taking pleasure in the clamor of crowds;
and their precepts are fully equipped according to the instructions of the Dharma, for they do not receive them from others.
"Be cautious and observe the prohibitions; do not use fine clothing for ostentatious adornment. Since no virtue can reach you, vow to remain as in your original aspiration.
Do not allow sweet flavors to disturb your mind."
Why is this? It is because the power of the Way subdues all evils.
Their conduct accords with the precepts, such that neither the devas nor the people fail to rejoice.
One practices the precept of loving-kindness in order to protect sentient beings;
one cultivates the precept of compassion in order to endure all sufferings;
and one observes the protective precepts in order to remain free from indolence.
Through the precept of equanimity, one bears both good and evil for the sake of all beings, because there is no dualistic mind.
One constantly examines the prohibitive precepts so as not to let them diminish, because one does not allow the mind to run wild;
through the precept, one does not contemplate evil nor spread the faults of others, because one protects all beings.
One firmly upholds the precepts because one does not allow the mind to follow its desires;
one accords with the precept of giving for the sake of nurturing all sentient beings;
and one practices the precept of patience because no [malicious] thoughts arise.
The precept of diligent resolve, because it does not turn back;
the precept of meditative reflection, because it attains stability;
and the precept of honoring wisdom, because one listens extensively to the true Dharma without satiety.
"The precept of cultivating extensive learning and the training rules, because it awakens one to the essential Dharma;
the precept of following virtuous teachers, because it leads to the penetration of all phenomena;
the precept of abandoning evil teachers, because it causes one to leave behind various false studies and unauthentic paths."
The precept of non-attachment to the body, because one knows that all phenomena are impermanent;
the precept of not craving life, because its meritorious karma is like purple-gold;
the precept of freedom from regret, because the mind is pure.
The precept of being without hollow pretension, because one trains in purity;
the precept of being without vexation or severity, because one’s intention is bright and free from defilement;
the precept of being without burning distress, because one does not scorch the body.
The precept of non-delusion, because it does not follow desire;
the precept of non-perilous burning, because it causes no harm;
the precept of non-aggression, because the mind is not distracted.
The precept of subduing the mind, because the intention is without error;
the precept of pervasive tranquility, because it is not abandoned by worldly activities;
the precept of conforming to the true and correct, because wisdom accords with the teaching.
They possess the precepts of all vows because they are fundamentally pure,
just like the precepts of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
Because it accords with the fundamental essentials:
just as the Buddha’s precepts of meditative concentration, he constantly maintains an impartial mind to deliver sentient beings;
this is the precept of entering the gateway to the Path through omniscience.
Why is this? Because they harbor no resentment.
These constitute the sixty-four matters of the pure prohibitions and precepts of a bodhisattva, which are inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati further addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses pure precepts:

he does not covet his own body, does not dwell upon all things, does not conceive of self or person, does not calculate a lifespan, does not contemplate name-and-form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and does not rely upon the four bases."
Earth, water, fire, and wind each have four great precepts:

not having eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and flavor, body and touch, or mind and phenomena; being without body, speech, or mind; and for those precepts to tend toward purity—this is the mark of single-mindedness without confusion or delusion.

Contemplate all dharmas with discernment: the precepts transcend emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and are likewise without form or image; they surpass the three realms, being neither attached to nor bound by them.
That precept does not involve such thoughts; therefore, it is not produced for oneself. Why is this?
Because there is nothing that arises. That which constitutes the precept is neither active nor inactive, fundamentally having no creation.
For this reason, the precepts have no divisions or boundaries; they abide in the middle, yet there is nothing upon which they abide.
Purity of mind constitutes the precepts, and consciousness has no place of dwelling.
Why is this? Because it is free from conceptualization.
Precepts are not bound by anything; the reason for this is that they are free from the power of desire.
Neither abiding in form nor being without form, yet equally conforming to the sensory world—this is called precept (*śīla*).
Being free from lust, anger, and delusion, and thereby liberated from ignorance and darkness—for this reason it is called precept.
Non-attachment and non-cessation, relinquishing the twelve links of dependent origination—therefore it is called precept.
Not conceiving of "what belongs to me," eliminating the self and the notion of self, and not dwelling in desire—therefore it is called precept.
It is without volitional action and free from seeking; it does not dwell upon perceptions of form, nor does it abide within any name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Therefore, it is called precept (*śīla*). It does not follow causes and conditions; it is without vexation and without harshness; it is neither self nor non-self, and it is not conjoined with doubt. Therefore, it is called precept.
Nor does one crave worldly blessings; yet it is not by being devoid of merit that one transcends all evils and unrighteous deeds.
Why is this? Because the ignorant act contrary to the Dharma, it is therefore called "precept" (śīla).
Being free from agitation and affliction, with both body and mind stilled, this is the characteristic of precepts.
One who reverently observes the precepts is like one whose illness has been cured; they do not sever the authentic scriptures and records of the Buddhas.
The Dharma-body is serene and cannot be exhausted; therefore, they do not sever the Dharma-body.
Why is this? Because there are no two types of karma:
first, non-attachment; second, non-interruption.
One does not sever the assembly of noble ones because one has attained liberation through its use.
One does not sever the various trainings. Why is this so?
"Because they accord with the prohibitions and precepts.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
"Because their fundamental nature is pure, it is inexhaustible."
What is meant by worldly precepts?
It means that even within the realm of birth and death there is an end. Why is this so?
Because they exist within the five destinies, they are called "exhausted.
The reason they are exhausted is that, due to coming and going, they do not abide in a single place.
As for the external immortals, those with the five supernatural powers, and those with worldly wisdom who seek superior longevity—their divine feet and lives come to an end.
Why is this so? Because precepts and prohibitions are subject to exhaustion.
Even the human precepts and the ten wholesome actions likewise have their end.
Why is this? Because it contradicts and abandons the precepts.
The precepts of all the gods of the desire realm are likewise subject to exhaustion.
Why is this? Because their merit has been exhausted.
The concentration and precepts of the various devas of the form realm are likewise exhausted.
Why is this? Because their concentration is disturbed.
Even the tranquil precepts of the formless realm devas are exhausted.
Why is this? Because their mental composure is wild and unruly.
Even the precepts of those on the path of training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and arhats are subject to exhaustion.
Why is this? Because it relies upon nirvana.
Furthermore, the precepts of the pratyekabuddhas are also subject to exhaustion.
"Why is this? Because they lack great compassion.
Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
"Only the Bodhisattva precepts alone are inexhaustible.
Śāriputra asked:
"For what reason are the precepts inexhaustible?"
Akṣayamati said:
"That which exhausts the precepts is not truly a precept;

therefore, the bodhisattva’s precepts are inexhaustible. Because his mind does not abandon all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), these are the precepts of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); because they ensure the lineage is never severed, they are inexhaustible."
What is meant by the "fruit of the path being inexhaustible"?
That which is called the "seed" refers to the bodhisattva-mind;
that which is called the "fruit" refers to the Buddha’s ten powers up to their inexhaustibility.
Therefore it is said that the bodhisattva precepts are inexhaustible.
Achalamati said to Śāriputra:
"The patience of a bodhisattva is also inexhaustible, for there are thirty-two matters [that comprise it]."
What are the thirty-two inexhaustibles?
One who is not attached to desire does not give rise to this thought:
"These are my wife and children," nor does he violate their bodies himself, nor cause others to violate them.
Therefore, patience is also inexhaustible. One does not dwell upon various evils, nor harbor resentment toward anyone;

one does not feel anger toward sentient beings, nor contemplate the faults of others. One does not contend with others, nor forget to assist them; even when subjected to slander or assault, one does not retaliate or mock.

One guards one’s own physical conduct and protects the multitude; being cautious of one’s own mind so as not to follow its whims, one constantly contemplates virtuous qualities and remains free from thoughts of craving and desire. Thus, one attains a majestic body, believing that good and evil deeds will inevitably yield their retributions. One refrains from false speech, and the mind remains pure.

The Bodhisattva’s mind is firm and does not abandon anything; he carefully reflects upon his own thoughts, and when his mind becomes inclined toward what is wrong, he immediately awakens to it and recognizes it. His mind is harmonious and supple, and he guards it so that evil does not arise.

Having cultivated pure conduct, they are born in the Brahma heavens; descending from the heavens, they return once more to the human realm, fully endowed with the primary marks and eighty secondary signs of excellence, and they attain a harmonious voice like that of Brahma.

To be liberated from lust, anger, and delusion; not to show a foul countenance or harbor resentment toward others; never to lose the merit one has cultivated; to subdue external scholars and various heterodox arts; to abandon all illnesses and avoid calamities; and to accord with and fulfill the path and teachings of all Buddhas—these are the thirty-two matters of the inexhaustible perfection of patience, which constitute the patience of a bodhisattva.
"What is meant by patience?
If one is reviled or insulted, one remains silent and does not respond;
if one is struck or beaten, one does not harbor thoughts of retaliation—this is called patience."
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the striker, nor does one see one's own body, for the staff is fundamentally empty.
If there is one who is angry, one harbors no resentment; regarding such speech as a magical illusion, when it arises, one does not give rise to a contrary mind, for one is able to subdue the will.
If one encounters those who harbor evil thoughts, if the mind does not know how to reflect upon it, one should think:
"This person brings forth evil; I ought not to emulate them.
When there is praise, do not be moved to joy.
Why is this? Because they do not give rise to the thought:
"I have gained a benefit."
Because he has subdued his mind, he does not feel sorrow or distress even when there is decline or loss;
because he is content with what he has, he does not regard the praise of others as mere flattery.
If there is slander, one remains unmoved. Why is this?
Because wisdom is vast and great.
Those who possess reverence do not become conceited, for their nature is cultivated in tranquility.
Even when performing prostrations, they do not feel elated, nor do they say:
"It is only right that you should do this."
If one attains power and status, one should not become arrogant. Why is this?
Because the mind remains unmoving.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, they do not feel weary or distressed even when in the midst of hardship and suffering, nor do they feel elated when in places of pleasure, because they clearly understand that all worldly affairs are impermanent.
"He is not shaken by the eight worldly concerns. Why is this?
Because he does not dwell within them, he never retaliates even when provoked by others, and thus no one dares to offend him."
Suppose there were someone who could endure having their body dismembered limb by limb, because they desire to fulfill the bodhisattva practices.

Even if their body were harmed, they would never harbor a contrary thought; for they understand that the body is a composite of the four great elements, destined for dispersal and extinction—how could it be worth coveting?
Why is this? It is because by virtue of this patience, one shall attain the body of a Buddha;
one endures all afflictions and incalculable hardships.
Why is this? It is because by means of this, one attains the power of the Great Peace and the Ultimate Path.

"If a Bodhisattva is among the ranks of brahmins, he manifests his body entering fire without being harmed; desiring to cause those people to know that their minds are pure, he transforms their deluded thoughts so that their wills turn toward the Truth, thereby enabling them to attain rebirth in heaven."

That brahmin was well-versed in and delighted in fire-worship; yet the manifestations of the Bodhisattva were such that nothing could alter them, for his virtue and wisdom were so transcendent that none could equal him. Why was this so?
The various Brahmās, Śakras, and the Kings of the Four Quarters prostrate themselves before the Bodhisattva and pay him homage.
Because the Bodhisattva’s forbearance is without limit or bottom, it is therefore called inexhaustible.
"Regarding those who revile him, he endures it without harboring resentment, nor does he think:
'Who is it that reviles me?
Through this tranquility, he immediately enters the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti)."
He does not reflect upon it thus:
"They are reviling my eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind.
If they revile the mind, where is that which is reviled?"
Thus, having transcended all decays, one immediately attains the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Not thinking of anyone at all who might come to revile them, they are able to enter immediately into the patience of non-persons (*apudgalakṣānti*).
All such patiences are, in fact, not patiences at all.
Why is this so? It is merely a provisional designation;
if one examines its "patience" (kṣānti) with discernment, it is like an echo in the mountains. One who understands this enters the patience of impermanence (*anitya-kṣānti*).
Not conceiving of attaining a self or attaining another, one attains the patience of the Middle Way (*madhyama-kṣānti*).
Nor does he think to himself:
"My body follows the teachings of the Dharma, yet I do not dwell in those dharmas; this is called patience.
I alone abide in the Path, while other people do not establish themselves in the Path."

He does not give rise to such thoughts: "I contemplate emptiness and do not contemplate reality; I contemplate the absence of ideation and do not contemplate the presence of ideation; I contemplate patience without remainder and do not contemplate patience with remainder; I contemplate patience without aspiration and do not contemplate having aspirations; I am patient regarding the absence of birth-and-death and do not regard it as having a beginning or an end; I am patient regarding what is acceptable and have no intolerance for what is unacceptable; I am patient regarding the possession of virtue and do not regard it as lacking virtue; I contemplate patience as being without arising and do not contemplate that which is born; I am patient in transcending the world and do not unite with the world; I am patient in entering the Path and do not regard it as being without the Path; I contemplate patience as liberation and do not regard it as being without liberation; I understand patience as *nirvāṇa* and do not regard it as being birth-and-death."
The Bodhisattva, practicing patience, does not give rise to such thoughts. Why is this?
Because they are unequal.
"What is meant by the 'patience of equanimity' of a bodhisattva?
To understand and enter into emptiness, wherein there is nothing to be severed and nothing to which one clings—this is the patience of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, they do not conceive of birth, nor do they conceive of non-birth, nor do they conceive of transformation-birth."

If there were no beings born by transformation, one would not give rise to thoughts concerning their existence or non-existence; because one thoroughly understands this principle to the point of inexhaustibility, it is called "inexhaustible."

Patience is entirely without action; one does not contemplate what ought to be or what ought not to be. There is nothing that manifests, neither bondage nor liberation, neither that which is produced nor that which brings about production. Therefore, because there is nothing produced, it is inexhaustible.
When one’s patience is such as this, it is called attaining the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).

From the time one calculates the attainment of this *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* until the Tathāgata sits beneath the Bodhi tree, one who enters this patience should receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), saying that they are inexhaustible.
When this "Chapter on the Endurance of Dharma" was being spoken, all those present in the assembly praised it, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
What Akṣayamati has said is truly without any difference from the truth."

At that time, one hundred thousand devas all made offerings with celestial flowers, famous incenses, banners, and canopies, scattering them over the body of Akṣayamati and upon the various bodhisattvas. Celestial musical instruments spontaneously resounded to provide entertainment for them. Each felt their mind expand and harbored a vast and magnanimous intention, and they all said:
"May all sentient beings universally attain the clarity of the Tathāgata’s patience; may those who hear this sound feel no alarm, no fear, and no anxiety in their hearts."
Various flowers, famous incenses, banners, and canopies filled and pervaded the entire trichiliocosm Buddha-field.
*The Sūtra of Akṣayamati Bodhisattva*, Fascicle Two.
*The Sūtra of Akṣayamati Bodhisattva*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Buddha addressed Acchuta: "O Benevolent One, are you now able to encompass all sentient beings?"
Aksayamati said: "I accept and shall fully undertake all that is entrusted to me by the Buddha’s holy command.

As soon as the Bodhisattva Aksayamati entered samādhi, at that very moment, all physical forms, offerings of flowers and incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers all entered through his navel; yet his body remained as it was before, neither increasing nor decreasing.
There was a bodhisattva named Mahāviśuddha who asked Akṣayamati:
"What is the name of the samādhi you have entered?

It is by manifesting such transformations that you are able to fully receive all physical forms, flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, yet your body remains as it was, neither increasing nor decreasing."
Aksayamati said:
"The name of that samādhi is 'Universally Receiving All Physical Bodies'.
Mahāviśuddha asked again:
“Does this samādhi only receive this, or does it receive other things as well?
Akṣayamati replied,
“The trichiliocosm enters entirely into the body, yet its location cannot be seen.”
Why is this? It is because of his majestic spiritual power that there is neither increase nor decrease.

At that time, the various assemblies—the devas, humans, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas—each had their own thoughts, like those who have long thirsted and yearned for a drink, desiring to see the miraculous transformations manifested by the Great Being.
The Buddha, knowing the minds of the assembly, said to Akṣayamati,
"Manifest this samādhi for the sake of all people.
Akṣayamati replied:
"I shall immediately uphold the holy teaching.

At that moment, the bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and the assembly of monks from the ten directions all saw themselves sitting within the navel of Akṣayamati. Within that navel there appeared a land named Samantavyūha; the robes of the bodhisattvas were like those of the bodhisattvas in the land of Samantavyūha, and they all likewise appeared within his navel, manifesting such a magnificent and sublime universal adornment.
Having manifested these majestic transformations, the assembly each sat down as before.
The Bodhisattva Mahāviśuddha addressed Akṣayamati:
"The noble grace and majestic virtue of this samādhi are so transcendent and extraordinary; its radiance is truly such as this."
Akṣayamati said:
"This is not worth mentioning. Why is that? Because—"

The three thousandfold world system, including its heavens, earths, mountains, and hills, is entirely received within his physical body as something trivial; he receives the soil of the Ganges sands without it being felt as cramped—how much more so for anything else?

When he preached the Chapter on Forbearance and displayed his supernormal powers, seventy *koṭis* of benevolent and virtuous people resolved their minds upon the Great Way, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Śāriputra asked Akṣayamati,
"I wish to hear further about the inexhaustible vigor of a bodhisattva.
Akṣayamati replied:
“Bodhisattvas have eight kinds of inexhaustible diligence. What are these eight?

First, donning the armor of the great virtue of the vast vow; this is diligence that is inexhaustible. Second, gathering and accumulating diligence without ever retreating. Third, diligently studying to nurture and increase all merits. Fourth, constantly desiring to nourish and provide for all sentient beings. Fifth, establishing the source of countless blessings and celebrations. Sixth, having no fundamental seeking in the various *pāramitās*. Seventh, clearly understanding wisdom without limit. Eighth, desiring to fully master all Buddha-dharmas, and for this reason it is inexhaustible. These are the eight kinds of diligence that are inexhaustible.”
Akṣayamati said:
"The reason he is called 'One Clad in the Armor of the Great Vow' is that he does not regard birth and death as toil or hardship. Why is this so? "
One does not calculate the number of kalpas required to attain the Buddha-way, nor does one dwell upon the thought of practicing the bodhisattva deeds for a certain number of kalpas.
The reason this is called a "great vow" (mahāpraṇidhāna) is that it is not limited by the vastness of immeasurable kalpas.

The Bodhisattva is still the foundation of all things, according to the reckoning of worldly conventions: one day to the fifteenth day, or thirty days, makes one month; twelve months make one year. Progressing in this manner up to a hundred thousand years, or even hundreds of thousands of millions of years, one resolves to seek the Way; yet even after such a number of years, one might only encounter a single Buddha.

In this manner, one may count as many Ganges rivers as there are grains of sand; all such beings, from those who have first resolved their minds and so forth, each give rise to the aspiration and each encompasses it. It is the same for as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges: incalculable and immeasurable numbers of people have all resolved their minds. What they know through their own intellects amounts to but a single matter, while that which they do not yet know is beyond measure.

It is as if one were to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and only thereafter fully complete the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), as well as the perfections of morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are likewise so.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s mind does not grow weary, nor does he cast off the great armor of his vast vows.
Jiangsha and the others all gave rise to the aspiration for the Way; by combining these merits, they were able to fully perfect one mark of a Great Man.

In this manner, through each of their respective prior efforts, they completely fulfilled all the marks of a Great Man—these "Great Men" being the Bodhisattvas—and yet, upon hearing this, the Bodhisattvas did not consider it a labor.
Why is this? Because they have never abandoned or contravened their armor of the great vow; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to don the armor of the great vow such that it is inexhaustible.
What is meant by the inexhaustibility of the increase of vigor?
If there is a bodhisattva who diligently desires to hear the Dharma, they do not calculate distance, nor do they loathe water or fire. Why is this?
Because they are free from weariness; the bodhisattva increases and accumulates merit without retreating, for they assemble and encourage the gathering of all merits.
For what reason do they assemble?
It is because they wish to transform and enlighten sentient beings, leading them across to liberation and causing them to enter *nirvāṇa*.

They enter *parinirvāṇa* without indolence; possessing a firm resolve that none can turn back, they constantly seek merit and virtue without weariness, always abiding in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); therefore, it is called "assembling."

Wherever a bodhisattva goes, whether walking, sitting, or rising, they do not forget the mind of the Way; for even the duration of a single thought-moment, they contemplate the Buddha’s teachings and protect all beings without finding it troublesome. Therefore, it is said that their accumulation is inexhaustible.
"What is meant by 'nurturing all diligence so that it is inexhaustible'?
It refers to the establishment of meritorious qualities and vows that always abide within the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); for this reason, it is called inexhaustible."
Just as when the various dragons rain down upon the great ocean, it is impossible to distinguish or know the number of drops—whether many or few—and they are incalculably inexhaustible;
so too are the merits of those possessed of all supernormal wisdoms, reaching to the point of being inexhaustible.
"What is meant by 'establishing immeasurable merit'?

It means that the mind applied to all activities is always maintained with equanimity for the sake of all beings; the meritorious deeds performed do not depart from transcendent wisdom; and the vows of cultivated blessings are intended so that all sentient beings may share in their grace. For this reason, it is called 'establishing immeasurable merit.'"
What is meant by seeking all the *pāramitās* with the mind?
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of sentient beings are entirely inexhaustible; those who are incalculable enter into these very calculations.

First, it is said that one teaches all classes of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm; such analogies are beyond measure and description. One transforms and enlightens *asaṃkhyeya* people in this infinite manner—hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-millionfold, and ten-billionfold, beyond all calculation or metaphor—and yet those whom one has taught and delivered are but a tiny fraction.
To hear this without fear, nor to be terrified or cowed, but to act with diligence—this is called establishing immeasurable merit that is inexhaustible.
What is meant by "understanding wisdom without end"?

Because the merits of a bodhisattva are inexhaustible, if one were to calculate all the merits originally performed by all sentient beings—ranging from those on the path of seeing (srotāpanna) through those who return once more (sakṛdāgāmin), those who do not return (anāgāmin), the non-attached (arhat), and the pratyekabuddhas—and were to combine all these merits, they would constitute the merit of a single hair-pore of a Buddha.
When the merits of each and every pore are collectively aggregated, these sublime and manifold virtues enable the formation of the mark between the two eyebrows;
a thousandfold the merit of such a mark between the eyebrows then forms the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.

Why is this so? Because within the heavens above and the world below, there is none capable of beholding the Buddha’s crown; for this reason, it is said that his virtue is inexhaustible and his wisdom is boundless.
"Furthermore, what is meant by 'wisdom that is inexhaustible'?

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to have profound faith in the Buddha; even if one’s faith in the Buddha were a hundred times greater than theirs, it would equal the merit of one who practices with devoted faith."

Even if those such as the *śraddhānusārin* were to fill the entire trichiliocosm, and their wisdom were increased a hundredfold, it would not equal that of one who has attained the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*).

Even if those who have attained the stage of the eight persons were to fill the entire trichiliocosm, and their wisdom were increased a hundredfold, it would not equal that of one established on the path of insight (*darśanamārga*).

If the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world were filled with people seeking the fruits of the path—those of the stage of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and the arhat—their combined wisdom, even multiplied a hundredfold, would not equal the wisdom of a single pratyekabuddha.
If the trichiliocosm were filled with pratyekabuddhas, they would still not equal the wisdom of a single bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment.

Even if the trichiliocosm were filled with such bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain enlightenment, their combined wisdom, multiplied a hundredfold, would not equal that of an avaivartika bodhisattva.

Even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and their wisdom were increased a hundredfold, it would still not equal the wisdom of a single bodhisattva who is in his final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).

Even if all the sentient beings in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were to become those in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and their wisdom were increased a hundredfold, it would not equal the power of the wisdom of a single Tathāgata in every respect.
Combining all powers and fearlessnesses, they enter the Buddha-dharma and roam within essential wisdom.
Why is this? Because all-encompassing knowledge is entirely contained within the Buddha’s mind.
When a bodhisattva hears this, they are not terrified, not afraid, not fearful, and do not find it difficult; this is called practicing inexhaustible wisdom that can never be exhausted.
"Why is it that the practice of infinite wisdom can never be exhausted?
It is because it enters into the minds of all sentient beings.

Even if the mental thoughts of past sentient beings were limitless, and a single person were to develop the aspiration for enlightenment, they would clearly understand and fully comprehend the mental thoughts of all those past sentient beings, treating them as if they were the mind of a single person; such analogies are beyond measure."

The classes of sentient beings are all shrouded by lust, anger, and delusion; furthermore, there is one person who enters into the midst of the confusion of lust, anger, and delusion, and is thus bewildered and lost amidst the turmoil of manifold defilements.

When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind, they constantly employ the wisdom of the Path to know that all sentient beings are in turmoil through lust, anger, and delusion; this is called the vast wisdom of the holy one’s luminous insight.

If all sentient beings each individually resolve their minds—whether regarding the causes and conditions of good and evil, or what is produced by those causes and conditions, whether arising or ceasing—a wise person such as this, though dwelling in the midst of these things, is not troubled by them, being able to penetrate them all with ease, just like empty space.
That which is space has no place that is not empty.

It is the same with noble wisdom: the mind’s clear understanding reaches all sentient beings of the three periods of time without exception; therefore, it is called wisdom that is infinite and inexhaustible.
"What is meant by 'all Buddha-dharmas are also inexhaustible'?
It means that one fully possesses all six *pāramitās* while seeking all Buddha-dharmas.

If a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, cultivates skillful means until finally reaching the sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, the merit of that initial resolve is beyond measure; it universally and completely fulfills all Buddha-dharmas. Therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva unites with all Buddha-dharmas and is inexhaustible."
Furthermore, there is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of diligence, which is likewise inexhaustible.

He does not consider it difficult to establish merit through his body; he does not grow weary in proclaiming his meritorious deeds with his speech; and he contemplates diligent cultivation with his mind. Thus, the diligence of these three matters—body, speech, and mind—is the very foundation.
What is meant by mental diligence?
It is when the mind is composed and serene.
What is meant by being composed and serene?
One seeks the Buddha-way by means of this.
What is meant by "seeking the Buddha-way by means of this"?
It is to expand the mind so that it is tranquil and devoid of purposeful action.
What is meant by "arousing this"?
To arouse this intention means to arouse the mind of enlightenment; this is the great compassion of the bodhisattva.
What is meant by the "stages of the bodhisattva"?
To have faith and delight in non-self is what is called patience (*kṣānti*).
What is meant by "arousing this"?
To arouse this is to be able to universally encompass all sentient beings.
"What is meant by 'abiding' (sthāna)?
It is because one attains the complete mastery of all dharmas that one does not regard birth and death as toil.
One who gives rise to this does not cling to the three realms."
One who gives rise to this has no attachment or stinginess regarding anything they possess.
Furthermore, as for their conduct, when giving, they do not boast or proclaim that they already possess such virtuous qualities;
that is to say, they do not praise themselves on account of their prohibitions and precepts, nor do they harbor a mind of self-importance.
Furthermore, as for that state, one endures all manner of suffering and affliction, yet does not harbor pride on account of such karma.
What is called "that state" is the merit obtained, which becomes ever more increased, vast and immeasurable.
What is called "abiding" is the resolve for liberation, never departing from giving, and subduing the mind and restraining the will;
what is called "abiding" is insatiability in study and training oneself in the teachings according to the Dharma;
what is called "abiding" is practicing the meanings as they have been heard without alteration and without harboring divergent thoughts.
What is meant by "abiding" (sthāna) refers to practicing and contemplating the ineffable Dharma, and regarding skillful means and expedients as not being difficult.

One practices without expectation, repeatedly studying, reciting, and chanting the Dharma that has been proclaimed; one contemplates and examines it until its ultimate purpose and destination are clearly understood, never becoming weary or indolent. One studies and cultivates with fundamental sincerity, without any thought of reward. These four matters constitute the practice of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because they are able to give rise to these [four immeasurables]: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Furthermore, as for their state, their contemplative mind universally embraces great pity.
Furthermore, by virtue of that state, one becomes fully endowed with the five supernormal powers and practices without birth or death;

moreover, by abiding in that state, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness and reaches accord with principle, such that one does not dwell upon what should not be contemplated and does not think of it.
Furthermore, as for that state, one knows the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) without abandoning merit, nor does one suppress those who lack blessings.
Why is this? Because one practices the middle way.
Furthermore, as for that state, it is the practice of the divine feet (ṛddhipāda), following the teachings of the Buddha-dharma without any expectation;
furthermore, as for that state, it is the cultivation of virtuous qualities, with the faculties undisturbed, and the ability to discern all limitless unrighteousness;
furthermore, as for that state, it is the ten powers (daśabala) which cannot be surpassed, and the mind harboring noble wisdom (āryajñāna).

Furthermore, as for that state: seeking the awakening of a Buddha, one undertakes all practices and enters into the meanings of the manifold dharmas without arrogance, thereby accomplishing the seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, as for that state: seeking this path of virtue, one does not dwell on those who come, stay, or depart, nor does one harbor any conceptualizations.
Furthermore, as for that state: aspiring to reverence and respect, one quiets the will so that it is free from confusion and distraction.
Furthermore, as for that state: one who desires right contemplation seeks to clearly examine all phenomena and investigate their underlying existence;
furthermore, one who has extensively heard the teachings is able to practice them, always abiding in accordance with the Dharma and striving to cultivate bodily virtue and conduct.
Furthermore, as for that state: seeking the Dharma-body while diminishing worldly conventions, one’s attachment to deluded thoughts gives way to faith in the formless;
furthermore, as for that state: regarding those sounds, one constantly desires to adorn them, so that they may flow forth at all times and penetrate the ten directions;
furthermore, as for that state: delighting in conduct like that of the Way, one causes both the liberated and the unliberated to reach eternal peace.
Furthermore, as for that state, it means not conforming to what is improper and transforming the four māras.
What are the four māras?
First is the māra of the body; second is the māra of the dust of transgressions; third is the māra of death; and fourth is the celestial māra.
"Furthermore, as for that state: it is to be free from all evil habits and to cultivate the roots of all virtues, so that all defilements are stilled and do not arise in disorder;
furthermore, as for that state: it is to universally perceive the wisdom of the Path and to examine the arising of all conditions;
furthermore, as for that state: it is to perceive all points of entry and worldly activities, employing the skillful means of regulation and adjustment to deliver beings through them."
Furthermore, as for those who dwell therein, they all perceive the Dharma and transform according to the times; this is the vigor of the mind that is inexhaustible.

"If there are those who can be complete in all places, they will ultimately encounter no difficulties; whatever they do will be fully understood. They do not abide in the wisdom of their practice through deluded thoughts, nor do they waver; all their actions remain inseparable from wisdom."
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s practice of never being separated from wisdom?
All the merits they cultivate are based on this Dharma, and they constantly give rise to boundless compassion for all beings.

This boundless compassion does not exhaust itself within the mundane world; because it relies on the wisdom of the Buddha-way, it does not follow the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). This is called the inexhaustible vigor of a bodhisattva.

When he proclaimed that diligence is inexhaustible, ninety-six koṭis of devas and worldlings all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and thirty-two thousand sons of gods all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.
Śāriputra again asked the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"Is there further meaning in saying that the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is inexhaustible?
Akṣayamati replied:
"By means of sixteen matters, one is inexhaustible, such that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot attain.
What are these sixteen?
First, in whatever one gives, one harbors no ulterior motives and fully accomplishes the Tathāgata’s gift of Dharma."
Second, when giving, one does not give rise to this thought:
"By reason of this, I shall obtain a karmic reward.
Third, one gives with universal compassion for all beings, harboring no discriminatory mind.
The fourth is: when practicing giving, one does not harbor thoughts of seeking the attainment of samādhi-samāpatti. Why is this?
Because one does not delight in being born in the heavens of the Śuddhāvāsa, but always prefers the human realm.
Fifth, in all that they give, they are able to fully comprehend the mental activities and conduct of sentient beings.
Sixth, their intention in giving is pure and harmonious. Why is this so?
Because he wishes to cause their minds to follow his own plans, he also causes their bodies to act according to what his mind intends.
Seventh: that which is given is in accordance with the recipient's wishes. Why is this so?
His virtue surpasses that of the gods of the form and formless realms.
The eighth is this: his giving is conjoined with tranquility and is likewise serene. Why is this so?
Because it surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Ninth: that which is given is not accompanied by a resentful mind. Why is this so?
Tenth, because he desires to bring [the practice] to ultimate fulfillment and accomplishment,
his exercised majestic spiritual power is so sublime that none can obstruct or sever it.
Eleventh, through the bestowal of wisdom, he treats all sentient beings with universal equality and establishes them in the crossing over of all.
Twelfth: That which is given, one gives to others with a heart of joy and gladness, and the mind of compassionate rescue remains constantly upright and at peace. Why is this so?
Because he is able to govern his mind.
Thirteenth: that which he bestows does not interrupt the Three Jewels. Why is this?
Fourteenth: Not abandoning the lineage of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.
Fifteenth: That which is bestowed is always luminous; one harbors no hesitation and remains free from delusion.
Sixteenth: That which is bestowed accords with the teachings of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because their practice accords with the meaning.
The sixteenth is: in whatever they bestow, there is nothing they do not know; in whatever they undertake, they delight in the root of wisdom.
Why is this? It is because one desires their wisdom to be inexhaustible and exceedingly vast.
This constitutes the sixteenth activity of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), which is inexhaustible.
"What is meant by dhyāna?
It is because the mind is tranquil.
What is meant by the supernormal powers (abhijñā)?"
Because of the perfection of wisdom.
What is meant by wisdom?
It is that whatever forms one perceives are not obstructed.
To behold all forms and yet have one's mind not follow them is called "penetration.
Why is this so? Because one does not seek realization midway along the path.
All that which is heard is non-attainment;
all sounds whatsoever are entirely ungraspable—this is called attainment.
To be able to fully understand the mental activities of sentient beings is itself non-attainment; one removes this knowledge from the mind and does not realize realization by exhausting the mind.
Why is this? Not grasping at arhatship is called "penetration.
To know for oneself the original cause from which one has come is not penetration; to have no obstruction regarding the three periods of time is called "penetration."
To pervade all lands is not yet penetration; though one pervades all lands, to understand that there is nothing existing and to be free from the notion of "lands"—this is called penetration.
To have faith in and incline toward all dharmas is not yet penetration; to realize and see the beginning and end of all dharmas—this is called penetration.
For all actions to be accompanied by a mind of false conceptualization is not yet penetration; to clearly understand sentient beings without any expectation—this is called penetration.

If one desires to be reborn there, yet it is obstructed by the various devas, Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings, this is called "non-penetration. A Bodhisattva knows all the noble wisdom cultivated by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and is able to master them entirely; this is called "penetration."

He is the leader of the multitude—what is called "leader" is so because he stands at the highest point among all dharmas—and for this reason, his merit of universal wisdom is said to be inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati further addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Because of various distracted thoughts, the bodhisattva habitually subdues his own mind; this is called dhyāna. That wisdom which completely abandons all evils is called samādhi."
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices and dwells in meditative concentration, the mind is unchanging. Why is this?
It is because they cultivate right dwelling; by cultivating right dwelling, they practice the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
Because they rectify all phenomena, those who practice all phenomena train by means of rectification;
they practice the bodhisattva conduct with a mind equal toward sentient beings, and having attained equality toward sentient beings, they attain equality toward all phenomena;
having attained equality toward all phenomena, they know the bodhisattva’s mind, and knowing the bodhisattva, they are able to fully comprehend the aspirations and character of sentient beings.
Having known sentient beings, one then knows all dharmas; this is called practicing the Great Equality (*mahāsamatā*).
All classes of sentient beings are entirely equal to all dharmas, without preference or aversion; dwelling equally in all dharmas is called the concentration of mind as right reception (*samādhi*).

Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are said to be equal to birth and death; that which is equal to birth and death is equal to all phenomena. Being thus equal, it is level and free from partiality.

When the mind is universally equal, it is equal to the minds of sentient beings; having become equal to the minds of sentient beings, it is then called "equality," and is therefore termed "universal equality."
"The movement of his mind is as level as empty space; like earth, water, fire, and wind, it is free from love or hatred.
His mind being thus equanimous, he is without sorrow or joy. His body already dwells in the Buddha-field of Animiṣa, and his concentration is like that of samādhi."

He does not dwell in flattery as he would in the ultimate limit; he is neither conceited nor self-deprecating, neither deluded nor malevolent, and neither loquacious nor verbose, desiring only to understand the fundamental source of all phenomena.

Whether it be the proper time or not the proper time, they always act in accordance with what is appropriate; they do not follow any of the defilements of the mundane world, but transcend the eight worldly concerns—gain and loss, defamation and praise, suffering and pleasure, fame and insignificance. Having abandoned all conditioned things, they take no delight in clamor and bustle; those who follow this Dharma do not depart from samādhi.

Why is this? Because they perceive all the practices established by beings in the world, and according to those practices, they continue to abide in samādhi such that no one can know them; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), which is the profound entry into the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and tranquility (*śamatha*).
"If one wishes to govern the mind through samādhi, it proceeds from infinite compassion according to causes and conditions.
Why is this? It is for the sake of sentient beings; this principle is called skillful means (upāya-kauśalya)."
The practice of samādhi that is tranquil and serene is called noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*).
To rely upon and look up to the Buddha’s wisdom according to what has been established by samādhi is called skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*);
whereas to never seek anything at all within all phenomena is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To uphold and maintain meditative concentration while transforming and protecting all dharmas through merit is called skillful means;
for the mind to be serene and unimpaired in its dharma-body is called wisdom.
To abide in samādhi while recollecting the various marks and secondary characteristics of the Buddha’s body is called skillful means;
to extensively bestow profound grace while recollecting the Buddha’s Dharma-body is called wisdom.
To recollect the Buddha within samādhi such that all sounds are like the voice of Brahmā is called skillful means;
to contemplate and know that all phenomena are devoid of verbal expression is called wisdom.
To abide in samādhi with a mind like a vajra is called skillful means;
though having attained meditative concentration, not forgetting the mundane world, sentient beings, and the multitude is called wisdom.
To maintain mindfulness within samādhi, to fulfill original vows, and to nurture all beings—this is skillful means according to circumstances and at the appropriate time;
furthermore, to contemplate in meditative reflection and realize that all sentient beings are entirely devoid of self—this is called wisdom.
To dwell in samādhi without abandoning any phenomena is called skillful means;
to understand that there is neither beginning nor end, and neither root nor source, is called wisdom.
To cultivate samādhi while contemplating all Buddha-lands as entirely pure is called skillful means.
To understand that all Buddha-lands are entirely non-existent is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To abide in samādhi and cultivate the adornment of the Buddha-tree alone is called skillful means (*upāya*).
For the body to be free from all desires and devoid of defilement is called wisdom.
Furthermore, to remain in samādhi while contemplating the turning of the wheel of Dharma is skillful means (upāya);
to practice meditative concentration while turning that which is not turned is called wisdom (prajñā).

To abide in samādhi, desiring to see the Bodhisattva adorned with the marks [of a great man], is called skillful means; to deliver all beings from suffering without the presence of afflictions (kleśa) is the dhyāna of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s dhyāna thoroughly understands all dharmas; it is forever free from craving and desire, does not conceive of worldly defilements, knows the pleasures of the senses, and eliminates all conceptualizations of phenomena. This is called meditative reflection, and it constitutes the wisdom born of the place where Bodhisattvas are born.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva employs single-mindedness such that it does not mingle with the defilements of dharmas, this is called the inexhaustible dhyāna.
Not allowing any of the Māras to find an opportunity, they thereby create various vessels of the Dharma for Perfect Enlightenment.
Why is this? Because there is nothing that it does not encompass.
While the True Being was thus expounding this inexhaustible perfection of tranquility (*śamatha-pāramitā*), forty thousand bodhisattvas attained the Sun-Light Samādhi (*sūryaprabha-samādhi*).
What is meant by the Samādhi of Solar Radiance?
It is like when the sun rises, the brilliance of lamps and torches, as well as the light of the stars and the moon, are eclipsed and rendered dark;
likewise, for a Bodhisattva who has attained this samādhi, all other holy ones are completely outshone.

Why is this? Because its wisdom is towering, luminous, vast, and expansive, it completely eclipses the intellectual illumination of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; for this reason, it is called the Sun-Light Samādhi.

The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati again addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What is meant by the 'Inexhaustible Perfection of Wisdom' (prajñāpāramitā) being inexhaustible?
It is called inexhaustible because one immediately establishes practice according to the wisdom as it has been heard."
There are eighty matters regarding how one should practice in this way.
What are these eighty? They are:
following what has been heard, investigating according to one's intention, training as taught, obeying the instructions of virtuous friends, and not being conceited.
Not forgetting what has been done; always being respectful and diligent; following the practice of the sutras; acting in accordance with the words [of the teaching];
repeatedly cultivating wisdom; receiving it with a diligent mind; not losing the proper measure; not forgetting mindfulness; having an undisturbed mind;
giving rise to the jewel-like intention; manifesting the resolve for medicine; removing all ailments; being a vessel of such an intention; delighting in patience; and reflecting with joy.
The truths; entering the wisdom-mind; studying without weariness; giving without longing for reward; giving without partiality toward friend or foe;
reflecting deeply on what is heard; receiving with joy and openness; the mind being glad and the body light; the mind being pure, harmonious, and free from vexation;
learning according to the original principle; always delighting in preaching the Dharma; hearing and desiring to turn toward the Path; the Dharma.
One who maintains self-restraint delights in hearing the correct Dharma and does not dwell among heterodox teachings; they receive only that which is elegant.
Having attained the *pāramitā* of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they reach the Vaipulya sutras of the Bodhisattvas, yet they merely aspire to hear the sutras of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, they delight in hearing and practicing the four immeasurable minds (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), while again examining and understanding that there are no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), remaining as they were at first, with no difference.
Mindfulness directs the mind toward the truths and skillful means; one desires only to hear the Dharma of non-arising, does not crave contemplation but delights in loving-kindness,
comprehends the twelve links of dependent origination, realizes impermanence, understands suffering, clarifies non-self,
seeks to know tranquility, discriminates emptiness, understands signlessness, embodies wishlessness, and awakens to birth.
Death, the full realization of merit, the penetration of sentient beings, knowing without forgetfulness, adorning one’s voice, being like a city wall, diligently grasping whatever is heard,
delighting in listening to the treasure of the sutras, knowing the mundane while remaining in the mundane, opening the inner mind to serve as a companion,
desiring to hear [the teachings] for the sake of subduing [defilements], and constantly aspiring toward all undertakings— universally.
Entering into all phenomena and aspiring to sever poverty—wherein "poverty" refers to a deficiency in wisdom, a lack of mindfulness and understanding, and failure to follow through with penetration;
it means to comprehend noble insight, joyfully accept the right path, and enlighten those who lack wisdom so that they may all know;
it means to realize the constant encounter with suffering, to provide for those in want, and to bring about the separation from all that is unmeritorious.
To recognize the root of virtuous deeds and clear understanding, to refrain from all evils, to promote the welfare of oneself, to benefit sentient beings through penetration,
to comprehend the practice of peace and security, to delight in freedom from resentment, to desire to distinguish the supreme and infinite matters,
and to contemplate the causes by which the various Buddha-dharmas are attained— this is called "wisdom that accords with what has been heard."
"Establishing Practice.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra:
"There are thirty-two matters through which a bodhisattva enters according to the occasion."
What are the thirty-two? First, entering according to sounds; second, desiring to enter contemplation; third, entering the movements of the mind;
fourth, entering the body to seek liberation; fifth, saving sentient beings; sixth, entering the uninterrupted impermanence; seventh, entering the non-abiding... [and so forth].
7. Attachment; 8. Entering that which is performed according to causes and conditions; 9. Entering the absence of a person (*pudgala*);
10. Entering the absence of a life-force (*jīva*); 11. Entering the absence of a soul (*jantu*); 12.
Entering the abiding place of the past, future, and present; 13. Entering meritorious karma; 14. Entering emptiness without indolence; 15. Entering the non-existent.
Fifteenth, entering into wishlessness while not ceasing diligent cultivation, one does not take realization through emptiness;
being without ideation or aspiration, one guards oneself so as not to fall [into lower realms].

Sixteenth, desiring to enter samādhi, one cultivates right reception (samyak-samādāna), directing all toward the accomplishment of samādhi and right reception, and for this reason, one is not reborn in the formless heavens.
Why is this? Seventeenth, it is because they provide protection and support;

eighteenth, furthermore, they enter the source of the wisdom of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), yet even so they do not enter the path of extinction (*nirvāṇa*); nineteenth, furthermore, they enter non-arising (*anutpāda*) to deliver all that has arisen; twentieth, they further enter the primordial limit (*koṭi*) to contemplate its meaning, desiring to enter the boundless while not taking realization as their goal.

Why is this? Because there is protection; whereas that which is called "without protection" refers to the śrāvakas (21). Furthermore, wishing to enter into sentient beings' understanding of non-self while not abandoning great compassion (22); entering into all fears and the perils of birth and death (23); although one enters and dwells within birth and death, it is for the sake of producing the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) (24); moreover, entering into what is loathed—namely, the various afflictions (kleśa)—(25); and entering into those who loathe desire yet do not fall away.
Why is this? Because they do not realize [nirvana] midway (26);

because they enter into the realm of inconceivable desire and enter into the non-abandonment of dharmas (27); because they enter into all transgressions of the law without committing wrongs (28); and because they enter into skillful means.

Why is this so? It is because, due to the causes by which sentient beings fall into craving and attachment, there are twenty-nine [teachings] for the purpose of opening their minds and transforming them; thirty, which were originally omitted; thirty-one, which consist of the instructions entered into according to the illness to provide the appropriate medicine; and thirty-two, wherein those saved by the Bodhisattva each attain their proper place. These are the thirty-two matters through which they are guided according to their respective needs.
Why is this? Because one does not lose the proper measure.
It is just as when one wishes to enter a city, one must enter through the gate.
If you wish to clarify the nature of all conditions, you should observe them with the eye of wisdom.

One who understands the workings of conditions does not engage in dispute; if you wish to bring about an end to contention, nothing is better than self-restraint. If you wish to know that silence is most excellent and pleasant, it is no better than simply remaining silent.

Why is this so? One who does not delight in speech guards their own body and mouth; one who does not desire to dwell does not reside in such places; one who does not desire to move carefully refrains from turning; and one who has no expectations likewise has no conceptualizations. For these reasons, they are called "equal."

If one wishes not to be deluded by forms, one should remain correctly and firmly established; having become firmly established, one will then reach the goal. One should not delight in change but always be self-restrained, aspiring instead to tranquility.
One who nourishes themselves should not boast of themselves;
one who does not wish to be lowly should not be self-exalting. Without being high or low, one is fully endowed with the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
One who does not delight in harming cannot be censured; if one finds joy in tranquility, whatever they do will be without failure.
One who has nothing lost has no doubt;
one who has no doubt understands that there is no fundamental basis, and thus has nothing lost, being equal throughout the three periods of time without distinction.

Those who are equal toward the three periods of time neither increase nor diminish anything; they do not abide in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they regard them as distinct or special.

When the eye perceives forms, its consciousness does not abide anywhere; likewise, the ear’s consciousness of sounds, the nose’s consciousness of fragrances, the tongue’s consciousness of flavors, the body’s consciousness of textures, and the mind’s consciousness of phenomena all do not abide anywhere.
From conduct that is fundamentally pure, acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with wisdom, in accordance with thorough investigation, and in accordance with selflessness:
to see the conduct of all phenomena as being without self is called wisdom;
to understand that all things possessed are actually nothing possessed, and that they are entirely without origin, is what is called wisdom.
Not to harbor arrogance because of one’s physical refinement is called wisdom (*prajñā*).

To know that a bodhisattva practices true and correct wisdom for the sake of attaining realization for the sake of all sentient beings—and to never abandon or depart from all phenomena for the sake of those sentient beings—is what is called a bodhisattva practicing wisdom.

The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said to Śāriputra: "When a bodhisattva practices wisdom and enters into all dharmas, thereby remaining without attachment, this is called prajñā."
There are sixteen matters that do not accord with wisdom.
What are these sixteen?
Because of ignorance, one gives rise to the yin and yang; from birth through old age and death, none of these accord with wisdom.
All his actions are likewise not in accord with the defilements, nor are they intermingled with the sixty-two views;

he neither exalts himself nor disparages himself. Whether there is gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or infamy, suffering or pleasure—he transcends these eight worldly concerns. Whether it be arrogance and self-importance, or humility and reverent caution—among these twenty-one worldly matters, he does not align himself with them.
Having removed all afflictions, he is not mired in ignorance; he awakens from the sleep of delusion, is liberated from all fears, and remains unjoined with transgressions or any mental impurities.
Because one does not eliminate the five aggregates, one remains within birth and death—conjoining with the demon of the body, the demon of transgression, the demon of death, and the celestial demon.
All sentient beings create causes and conditions without any expectation of self, person, or life-span;

yet all expectations, worldly thoughts, notions of "it being thus" or "not thus," and matters of right and wrong are all fetters of karma. To harbor such greedy attachments is to act in opposition to the precepts.

Those who do not uphold the prohibitive precepts and those who do uphold them; patience and anger, diligence and indolence, single-mindedness and distracted thought, wisdom and ignorance—all these are transcended through the *pāramitās*. Likewise, arrogance and humility are both abandoned in this way.

One who abides firmly in non-abiding is called a *brāhmaṇa*; with a resolute and steadfast mind, possessing both strength and flexibility in virtue, they eliminate all discursive thoughts until none remain, thereby entering the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding the excellence or inferiority of lands, the fortune or misfortune of sentient beings, all that is wholesome or unwholesome, the clarity of ignorance or wisdom, birth-and-death or extinction, the truths and what are not truths—one who is wise remains detached from all such thoughts; they have nothing to perceive, no vision, and no signs, and they do not even conceive of nirvana.
"What is meant by wisdom?
It is to examine and deliberate upon the eight dharmas, and to clearly understand the merits of these eight dharmas. What are the eight?"

He was enlightened regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), understood the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), comprehended the six sense-decays (*āyatana*), distinguished the four truths (*satya*), and attained penetration into the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). He clearly elucidated the three periods of time and recognized all arhats and pratyekabuddhas; reaching the stage of a bodhisattva, he expounded all dharmas.
"What is meant by 'understanding the five aggregates'?

All that arises and ceases is like an illusion or a magical transformation, like what is seen in a dream, a plantain tree, a mirage, an echo in the mountains, a reflection in a mirror, or a bubble on the water."

Contemplating all forms, the self, the person, and the life-span, one understands form to be thus: sensation is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, volitional formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is reckoned to be like an illusion—like a water bubble, a mirage, a plantain tree, or a magical transformation.
Why is this so? Because it is subtle and wondrous.
That which is subtle and wondrous is without self and without person, without life-span and without vitality; this is the understanding of the five aggregates.
The self, the person, and the life-span are like an illusion; consciousness, too, is like an illusion—this is the understanding of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The five aggregates fall into the mundane; that which is characterized as worldly appears for a moment and then vanishes—this is called the characteristic of the world.
As for these worldly phenomena, they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and not the work of a self; one who knows this is said to have understood the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
What is meant by "comprehending the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind"?

As for that dharmadhātu: it does not become solid or rigid; water is not present within the dharmadhātu; fire does not heat itself within the dharmadhātu; and wind does not cause movement within the dharmadhātu.
Regarding those four great elements: that which is cognized by the eye is reckoned within the dharma-realm; one does not view with the eye, yet views and knows all. As for that dharma-realm:

one does not hear sounds with the ear, the nose does not seek fragrances, the mouth does not savor flavors, the body does not feel tactile smoothness, and the mind does not cling to dharmas; it fully understands the dharma-realm and is entirely complete therein.

As taught regarding the *dharmadhātu* of sentient beings, one praises their emotional dispositions and natures: the *dharmadhātu* is equal, as equal as a scale. The *dharmadhātu* of the desire realm is also equal as a scale; the *dharmadhātu* of the form and formless realms is entirely equal as a scale. The realm of birth and death, the realm of *nirvāṇa*, and the realm of the *dharmakāya* are equally balanced like space; the *dharmadhātu* is likewise so.
Why is this so? Because those with virtue and those without virtue are equal like space, without distinction; they are immeasurable and entirely beyond description or calculation.
The realm of Nirvana is likewise thus, and cannot be fully expounded.
This entry into the Dharma-realm is called wisdom; it is designated as the thorough understanding of the four great elements.
What is meant by "understanding the six decays"?
It is as explained in this statement:
That eye is also empty; it is neither possessed of a self nor devoid of a self, for even this is entirely empty.
Why is this so? One who understands the emptiness of the self remains amidst the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*) without being affected by them; this is what is called understanding the six decays.
To discern the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana) as neither attached to nor severed—this is for a bodhisattva to understand the six sense-bases.
The eye and forms constitute a sense-base; that which is seen does not fall [into error].
Why is this? Because they do not realize [enlightenment] midway.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the bodhisattva’s understanding of the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
What are called the six decays?
One who is able to discern the six decays, and having distinguished the six decays, enters the Way; one who does not distinguish the decays does not possess the Way.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva employs great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they are neither near nor far;
because of sentient beings, they do not abandon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) nor depart from giving (*dāna*). This is called the bodhisattva’s understanding of the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
"What is meant by the distinct Four Noble Truths?
To know that suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path do not abide within the five aggregates is called knowing suffering.
That which is produced is the origin; that form appears and is immediately extinguished is called cessation."
Because one attains the Way while the mind of non-Dharma abides in equanimity, it is called "the Way.
The Bodhisattva knows the Four Noble Truths but does not realize them. Why is this?
Because it protects all, this is called the specific discernment of the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, there are three matters. What are these three?

The characteristic of ultimate truth is thoroughly understood as it is in its original state; conventional reality is merely a provisional designation of names. When one realizes ultimate truth, the mind does not conceive of existence or non-existence.
To thoroughly understand the original state is for all forms to be entirely equal.
"Why is this? Because one does not realize the truth through the Middle Way, but instead takes up signs as a correspondence; this is what is called being distinct from the Four Noble Truths.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"The Truth is one; there are not two. Why is this so?

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has no expectations and does not conceive of or seek after form or the formless; having no expectations, he thus attains the realization that these are the four distinct truths."
"Furthermore, the suffering of the five aggregates is the characteristic of affliction; one who delights in understanding emptiness is said to realize the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
To thoroughly comprehend how the five aggregates arise from conditions is called the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya)."

All things perceived possess the impulse of conceptual seeking; to discern their underlying intent and remain free from craving and longing, yet not to forget even that which is not sought—this is called the meaning of equal knowledge and the total cessation [of grasping].
Not associating with the objects of the past, future, or present, nor dwelling within them— this is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
For one who seeks to attain the Path, to fully comprehend that suffering, its origin, and its cessation do not reside in two things— namely,
the two things being hesitation and the web of fetters— this is called the Truth of Cessation.
"To observe them with discernment and know that they are suffering—this is how a bodhisattva distinguishes the Four Noble Truths.
To perceive all that is seen as suffering, pleasure, good, or evil, and for the mind to fully comprehend the beginning and end of the world—all this is called 'knowing suffering.'"
That all conditions are suffering is called "origination.
To understand and renounce the suffering of the world so as not to seek it, yet without falling into the realization of extinction—why is this so? Because:
Because one does not seek realization midway, this is called the bodhisattva seeking the Way through knowledge.
It is like one who wishes to cross a river but finds no boat; unable to swim across, they contemplate a means:
"If I can find a plank, by mounting upon it I may be able to cross."

Why is this? Because one does not grieve over what has not been crossed, nor does one lament remaining in suffering; practicing and abiding in this manner according to the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, one does not fall into grasping at realization by contending over form—this is called the Bodhisattva’s discernment of the Truths.
To contemplate that suffering arises from the mind, and that suffering arises from conditions yet does not arise from conditions—this is called knowing arising.

That all which is produced is actually non-produced, that there is no agent of arising, and that there is neither extinction nor the intention to cause extinction or cessation—this is called the stilling of the mind, whereby suffering is extinguished.
Delighting in knowledge and seeking excellence, one subdues the mind; when the intellect understands and enters this state, it is called "knowing the Way without dwelling within it.
Why is this? Because wisdom has no abode;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s distinct knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.
"What is meant by 'attaining mastery over the twelve links of dependent origination'?
It means that because of ignorance, one comes to birth and death; as taught in the various Dharma discourses, whatever arises cannot be seen and cannot be known."
Why is this so? Because there is no arising, nor is there non-arising; by thoroughly understanding such matters of causes and conditions, one seeks nirvāṇa through conditions.

One clearly perceives that the practices of sentient beings are not uniform—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and that they create the path of practice based on the commission of sins or merit. That which ought to be attained is the arousal of the condition of non-arising; to cultivate the karma of all dharmas and harmonize with the Way is what is called "understanding the twelve links of dependent origination."
If these conditions do not exist, then they are extinguished; what is called "extinguishing" refers to the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The cessation of ignorance means the cessation of old age, sickness, and death. One who is able to realize this has understood the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

All causes whatsoever are subsumed within the Dharma; all conditions whatsoever are conjoined with the Dharma. The conjunction of these causes and conditions is neither self nor other, nor is it a person, a life-force, or a soul; it is entirely without entry.
One who enters in this manner does not abide in any existing phenomena; their mind universally understands these twelve links of dependent origination.
The Bodhisattva desires to fully perfect all dharmas;
having perfected all dharmas, they realize their impermanence and do not fall into premature realization.
Why is this? Because they protect sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva’s understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination.
What is meant by “clarifying the three periods of time”?
Fully knowing the intentions of others—whether they possess virtue or lack it—and regarding one's own body and others as equal without distinction.

Why is this? Because when the body commits an error or another person commits a transgression, one repents on their behalf; having attained the merit performed, one generates the aspiration for the Way by means of that karmic blessing. This is the past merit of a bodhisattva.

Whatever merit one performs with the intention directed toward the future, all of it is used to give rise to the resolve and establish the vows of a bodhisattva; all such resolved intentions are guarded, restrained, and maintained, and by holding the mind firmly so as not to admit turbid thoughts, this constitutes future merit.
