It is when consciousness does not abide in the ground of the five aggregates, and one cuts off all the veils of the aggregates—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is called wisdom.
Furthermore, that which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) is the clear discernment of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind.
If consciousness functions without dwelling in these four, does not race about, and does not destroy the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), this is called "wisdom" (prajñā).

Furthermore, that which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the attachments to what is cognized by the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena; this is termed consciousness.
If one eliminates these, so that the mind does not wander outwardly and is guided by wisdom such that there is no longing for any phenomena, this is termed "wisdom" (prajñā).
When there is reliance and attachment, consciousness arises; it also arises from conceptualization, longing, and much seeking—this is called consciousness.
If there is nothing received and no longing, if the mind harbors no thoughts, has no objects of desire or pleasure, and the will does not hope for reward—this is called wisdom.
Conditioned phenomena abide within consciousness;
when one cultivates unconditioned practice, consciousness has no place of abiding. To uphold the light of the unconditioned is what is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
If one abides in the factors of arising, it is termed consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Non-arising and non-ceasing, with consciousness having no place of abiding—this is called wisdom.
What is meant by grasping the meaning of the sutras?
What is meant by grasping?
To diligently and earnestly seek among the various scriptures is called grasping;
if one attains the fruits of the Path through the scriptures, this is called grasping the meaning.
If one accomplishes all practices through the various scriptures, this is called grasping.
If one can discern the beginning and end of various sutras, this is called grasping the meaning.
If one enters into the cultivation of karmic practices within various sutras, this is called grasping [the form];
if, regarding various sutras, one extinguishes both demerit and merit and forever eliminates worldly afflictions, this is called grasping the meaning.
If one extracts essential wisdom from various sutras and explains the karmic activities of afflictions to others, this is called grasping at the letter;
if one clearly discerns the pure passages and chapters within various sutras, this is called grasping the meaning.
If, regarding various sutras, one feels weary of the hardships of birth and death and is distressed and unhappy by them, this is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
To observe both birth and death and extinction (*nirvāṇa*) within various sutras as not being two distinct things—this is called "grasping the meaning."
If, regarding the various sutras, one merely proclaims miscellaneous phrases and ornate teachings, this is called grasping at the letter;

if, regarding the various sutras, one delights in their profound meaning, which hooks into the abstruse and reaches the far-reaching, being serene and unconditioned, this is called grasping the meaning.
If, regarding the various sutras, one conceives of and cognizes them as being innumerable, and directs the mind toward sentient beings, this is called grasping;
if, regarding the various sutras, one delights in knowing them while the mind gives rise to nothing, this is called grasping the meaning.

If, regarding the true sutras, one calculates in terms of a self, a person, or a life-span; if sentient beings harbor likes and dislikes and give rise to expectations; or if one asserts that what is spoken therein has no master, yet forcibly establishes a fundamental origin, a sovereign, or a master—this is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).

If, regarding the various sutras, one understands the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; if one does not give rise to [thoughts of] arising or birth, and there is nothing at all to be practiced; and if one does not calculate in terms of a self or a life-span, but expounds the three gates of liberation—this is called "grasping the meaning."
"What is meant by 'dharmas' and what is meant by 'persons'?
If one is attached to persons, from what source does one cultivate dharmas? This is what is meant by being a person."
If one exists as a person and dwells within the sensory realms without relinquishing the various dharmas, this is called "clinging to dharmas.
Furthermore, that which is called a "person" refers to the nature and conduct of ordinary, common folk; thus they are termed persons.

If one among ordinary persons honors the meaning of the True Persons, cultivates sincere faith, and upholds the scriptures, they are joined with the eight types of persons: those on the path of stream-entry, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, those who go and return, those who do not return, those who are free from attachment, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there appears in the world another person who brings great compassion and provides great peace and security; he takes pity upon the three realms—the devas, the people of the world, and those in the three evil destinies—and there is none who does not receive his salvation. He is named the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata, the Truly Real One, brings universal peace to all; he reveals the path and transforms the common people so that they may enter the meaning of the Way.

Should there be those who rely upon and cling to seeking [protection from others], they would have no refuge. Because he wishes to enlighten such deluded ones, he therefore says this: "One should take refuge in the Dharma; do not take refuge in persons."
One who calculates according to the Dharma performs no conditioned activity; there is no identical form, no doing, and no non-doing. Abiding in non-abiding, it is likewise without root.
One practices universal equanimity, being equal toward the True and Right, and also equal toward perverse karma.
To equate the heterodox with the orthodox and the orthodox with the heterodox; for heterodoxy and orthodoxy to be non-dual, free from all expectations and entirely devoid of practice;
to attain spontaneity regarding all phenomena, whose ultimate characteristic is like empty space—this is called the Dharma.
One does not even think of the teachings that have guided them as being a source of personal favor.

If one enters the meaning of this Dharma-gate, one perceives all phenomena as the Dharma of the Path; thus, one masters all phenomena without weariness. This is the inexhaustible meaning of the four refuges of the Bodhisattvas.
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Five.
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Akṣayamati said: "Indeed, Śāriputra! The karmic deeds of a bodhisattva’s merit and the karmic deeds of their noble wisdom are likewise inexhaustible.
What are called the deeds of merit?

If one can practice giving by renouncing all that one possesses, maintain the virtue of the precepts, cultivate the karma of the wisdom of the Path, constantly practice a compassionate mind, contemplate with a concentrated mind, exercise boundless pity, and uphold the roots of all goodness.

Practicing giving for oneself as well as for others, one gathers merit and exhorts all sentient beings of the three periods of time to give; this extends universally to those who are training and those who are beyond training, as well as to those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. One further encourages and assists those who have first resolved their minds to study the Bodhisattva path, from those entering the stages of practice up to those at the stage of non-retrogression and those in their final birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha). One universally exhorts the Buddhas of the past, future, and present regarding the blessings resulting from the roots of virtue they practice, and offers prayers that all Buddhas, sages, and Dharma-preachers may endure long and possess infinite lifespans through these merits.
He exhorts the multitude toward the roots of virtue; though these may bring merit and fortune, he does not merely encourage them, but inspires them to resolve for the Bodhi-mind.
For those who have already resolved their minds, he causes them to reach the Perfection of Deliverance.
If there are those who are impoverished, he rescues and sustains them with material wealth.
To those whose bodies are afflicted by illness, they provide medicine and supplies, making offerings at all times without harboring flattery or deceit;
to those who are weak and inferior, they encourage them to establish themselves in patience;
and to those who conceal their transgressions, they cause them not to hide their faults, but to always maintain a sense of shame and openly reveal their misdeeds.

He reveres and honors all Buddhas of the present and past; with love and respect, he takes refuge in his teachers and preceptors; he constantly practices the gift of Dharma to transform those who have no master; and he diligently cultivates vigor, seeking the Dharma without indolence.

“Whenever he saw Dharma masters, he regarded them as Buddhas; he listened to the Dharma without weariness, cherishing it in his heart. Hearing that there was a scripture far away, fourteen thousand *li* distant, he personally set out for it without considering it a hardship.”

Although he preaches the sutras and the Dharma, he does not crave gain or offerings; he is filial toward his parents, providing for them morning and night without leaving their side, constantly mindful of the repeated kindness of nursing him at the breast.
Without harboring resentment, they accumulate merit without weariness; their physical conduct is prudent and disciplined, and their bodies are free from ornate adornments.
They constantly guard their speech, refraining from coarse words; they maintain their own intentions, and their minds harbor no malice.
To establish Buddhist temples and lecture halls, the meritorious reward obtained is like that of Brahmā.
What is meant by "Brahma-merit"?
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment and was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the various devas solemnly came to offer encouragement and assistance:
"Originally, for the sake of all those wishing to cross over, the five rivers and three sources of the ten directions flow and overflow without ceasing.

I vow to uphold my original oath to open the way and deliver all who are deluded, blind, and inverted; those caught within the sixty-two views of the upper and lower realms, and those submerged and confined within the ninety-six paths—only the Great Sage can rescue them with his brilliance."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, O Heavenly King, you harbor such compassion.
The world of the five turbidities is extremely difficult to transform; one must employ the three vehicles to guide and advance beings, and only then can they enter the unsurpassed Great Way."

"The merit of this Brahmā is beyond measure; the merit of establishing a Buddhist temple is likewise so. By accumulating immeasurable deliverances through these meritorious deeds, one becomes fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
by practicing the roots of various manifold virtues, one thereby fulfills the eighty secondary characteristics."
“Practicing the ten wholesome paths without arrogance adorns the body, making it upright and beautiful;
abandoning all evil speech and coarse words adorns the mouth with eloquence;
and constantly maintaining a mind of loving-kindness without harboring malice adorns the mind, pure as a bright pearl.”

They adorn Buddha-lands through supernatural transformations; they adorn the scriptures by expounding them for others; they adorn assemblies so that all may uphold the Way and its teachings; and they abandon and eliminate double-tongued speech, harsh words, slander, and inciting strife.
He consulted and received the sutras, observing them with the thought:
"By what means may they be delivered and led to the Great Way?
In whatever he proclaimed, he never transgressed the proper order, nor did he act with partiality; his countenance was always serene and joyful.
When the multitude saw this, there was none who was not filled with joy; they cut away their lower garments and listened to the sutra with single-minded devotion.

Their minds became clear and sharp, which served as their adornment. They prostrated themselves and took refuge in the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, making the adornment of the *bodhimaṇḍa* and the fundamental roots of all virtues their primary focus. They purified the places where they were born, and guarded against transgressions and merits, as well as craving, desire, and the afflictions of worldly toil.

Having attained the Treasure Hand, one is able to bestow all manner of precious treasures upon others without expectation; by giving with such inexhaustible wealth, one attains an endless and vast treasury of jewels.
"With a face always serene and joyful, never showing a look of sorrow, his friends, companions, associates, and fellow students were all pleased with him.
By treating all sentient beings with an impartial mind, he attained a levelness as smooth as the palm of a hand."

Do not disparage those who have not yet studied; take joy in offering lamps to Buddhist temples so that parents, teachers, and friends may obtain pure radiance that illuminates all things, and accumulate merit while upholding the precepts without any stain.

In every lifetime and wherever they are born, they dwell in pure places and do not propagate the impurities of others; if they are in the womb, they are always free from defilement. By practicing the ten wholesome paths, they are reborn in the heavens, and when returning to the human realm, they never harbor thoughts of any web of fetters. For this reason, they walk alone, free from all falsehood.
"His instruction is without reliance on teachers or laws; therefore, among all phenomena, he is most supreme and noble.

His nature and disposition are pure, such that the people of the entire world never tire of beholding him. He does not spare his own body or life, has never deceived others, and commits no acts of aggression or injustice."
Because they have fully accomplished all the dharmas of the Buddha-way through their original vows, they are thus endowed with the roots of all virtues.
"It is so, Śāriputra!

By establishing these roots of virtue and nurturing them according to the occasion, one obtains immeasurable blessings; moreover, they exceed this beyond measure and cannot be fully described. I have merely set forth the essentials here and shall not elaborate upon them in detail."
"What is meant by the causes and conditions from which the karma of wisdom arises, such that one receives a spiritual consciousness and attains the five supernormal powers of wisdom?
What is meant by 'cause' (hetu)?
What is meant by 'condition' (pratyaya)?"

Those who possess great desire for the Dharma constantly seek the Buddha-dharma; with wise and virtuous friends always accompanying them, they consult, receive, revere, and uphold the wisdom of the Buddha. They do not seek the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and they remain free from arrogance. They honor them as supreme saints and revere them as Perfectly Awakened Ones. Their will and nature are harmonious and well-adjusted; when they behold their spiritual kin, they follow the meaning of wisdom rather than clinging to mere words. Seeing the various factors of the path practiced by the Dharma masters, they do not delight in external forms. Hearing the teachings they preach, they diligently practice the instructions of the Dharma. Such practitioners of the Dharma constitute the "karma of wisdom."
"What is called the karma of the Dharma?

It is to aspire to few desires and not be driven by frantic pursuit; to be sparing in greetings and brief in speech; to constantly awaken oneself and practice with diligence; to contemplate and weigh the meanings one has heard; and to never grow weary or indolent in one's thirst for the Dharma."
His mind is clear and bright, not obscured by the five hindrances; he regrets his transgressions, dissolving all calamities, and his intent is simple and honest, free from flattery or deceit.

Taking practice as the essential, they love the Dharma and delight in the Dharma; taking the Dharma as their foundation, their every movement is in accordance with the Dharma. They constantly seek the meaning of the sutras, as if their hair or skin were on fire, striving to extinguish it.

Diligently cultivating the self and practicing the fundamental principles without ever straying from them, they hasten toward the sublime and cast off disorderly associations; dwelling alone in a solitary place, they delight in seclusion, practicing the conduct of the benevolent and wise, exercising moderation and contentment without ever regressing.

Delighting in the joy of the Dharma and not coveting worldly glory, he seeks the way to transcend the world with a resolve that is never forgotten; in every movement and gesture, he always delights in essential meanings, seeking the practice of gentleness and accumulating steadfast essentials.

Constantly harboring a sense of shame and remorse, they cultivate agility of mind, mindfulness, and wisdom; they dispel all lack of knowledge, cast off the net of ignorance and blindness, and purify the eye of wisdom.

That which he awakens to is exceedingly vast and far-reaching; with the wisdom of the unconditioned, his noble mind shines afar upon present wisdom and future merits. He does not proclaim his own fame but praises the merits of others; he skillfully cultivates the noble deeds and, never departing from [the understanding of] transgression and merit, he purely cultivates the path of wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are four matters through which the activity of wisdom is attained by means of giving:

first, the giving of paper and bamboo silk; second, the giving of brushes to enable the copying of sutra texts; third, the giving of fine ink and superior inkstones; and fourth, whatever various dharmas the Dharma Master expounds, one receives and accepts them all from him, as they are difficult for the entire world to attain."

One who makes offerings to the Dharma Master, or bestows verses and hymns upon others, or grants sublime Dharma to the Dharma Master, doing so with sincere devotion and free from flattery—by practicing these four kinds of giving, one achieves the karma of wisdom and attains five qualities: faith, precepts, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"One shall protect and maintain four kinds of wisdom and thereby attain mastery. What are these four?

First, protecting and maintaining the Dharma Master as one's teacher; second, protecting and maintaining one’s lineage so as not to give rise to a distracted mind; third, protecting and maintaining the minds of the people in the land and its villages; fourth, guarding one’s own mind so that it does not wander. These are the four matters."
“Furthermore, there are four matters for approaching the work of wisdom that cause one’s virtue to be perfected.

What are these four? First, to offer profound sūtras to the Dharma Master; second, to diligently approach the meaning of wisdom day and night; third, to provide clothing and food to relieve their deficiencies; fourth, to gradually approach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) without turning back. These are the four.”
It is by reason of this that the wisdom of the five powers is attained.
What are these five? The first is called the power of faith;
The second is the power of liberation, which consists of not abandoning diligence and never tiring of extensive learning;
the third is the power of intention, which consists of not forsaking the mind of enlightenment;
the fourth is the power of concentration, which consists of viewing all phenomena with equanimity.
The fifth is the power of wisdom, which consists in not forgetting what has been heard;
these are the five powers.
Furthermore, there are four matters concerning the activity of the power of ethical discipline and wisdom.
What are the four?

First, to abide in the Dharma with truthfulness and practice the fundamental precepts; second, to contemplate the scriptures and examine where their meanings converge; third, to exhort and assist others toward the path of true correctness through the Dharma; fourth, to strive to seek essential teachings and take the Dharma as one's precept. These are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four matters regarding the practice of patience in wisdom. What are these four?
First, one diligently seeks the Dharma; even if others treat one with malice, reviling and abusing one’s person, one endures it all.”
Second, those who love and delight in the Dharma are able to endure all encounters with strife and litigation, hunger and thirst, and cold and heat;
third, they honor and respect their virtuous teachers and comply with the instructions of their preceptors;
fourth, they fundamentally contemplate the Dharma, enduring the meanings of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four matters regarding the practice of diligent application:

first, to diligently seek out and listen to the sutras without becoming weary; second, to grasp and retain what has been heard without ever forgetting it; third, to cultivate the preaching of the Dharma with diligence without negligence or desistance; fourth, to fundamentally practice these as one's primary vocation. These are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four matters regarding the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
first, the faculties and mind are tranquil and free from clamor;
second, one constantly maintains a single-minded focus, remaining undivided by pleasure or pain.”
The third is to single-mindedly and with focused devotion seek all supernormal powers;
the fourth is to enter the Buddha’s wisdom and eliminate mundane knowledge.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four matters regarding the practice of wisdom:
first, not abiding in annihilationism;
second, not dwelling in eternalism."
The third is that his mind is not deluded, clearly understanding the root of dependent origination without confusion;
the fourth is that he has faith in the absence of a self. These are the four.
"The skillful means of the wisdom-karma further comprise four matters:

first, to transform those who delight in worldly dharmas by following conventional customs; second, to draw in those who calculate the existence of a self by accommodating them; third, to gradually induce and advance them by means of the path of the scriptures; and fourth, to deliver through clarity those who cultivate wisdom and understanding. These are the four."
“The karma of the wisdom of the Way further consists of four matters:

first, practicing the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) to attain the ultimate Way; second, through mastery, returning to the end [of suffering] and dwelling within the transformation of the Right Dharma; third, training the mind and harmonizing the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga); and fourth, constantly advancing to follow and practice the root of all wisdom. These are the four.”
“There are four further matters regarding tirelessness in the noble practice:

first, never being weary of hearing the Dharma; second, proclaiming the scriptures without weariness or difficulty; third, investigating the origins of afflictions and trials without considering them a burden; and fourth, clearly understanding lofty principles with thorough mastery and without fatigue. These are the four.”
Akṣayamati spoke again:

"One who is able to enter into this universally should correctly contemplate the karma of giving, as well as that of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, wisdom, and loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."

Why is this so? Although a bodhisattva has not yet accomplished all [qualities], they take wisdom as their foremost priority to serve as the ground of the sages; they fully return to the Way and abide in right wisdom. They transform those who lack the meaning of wisdom, causing them to return to the Mahāyāna. No demons whatsoever can find an opportunity against them, and they are all established by the Buddhas to reach the unsurpassed, true, and correct state of omniscience (*sarvajñā*). This is the inexhaustible karma of the bodhisattva’s noble wisdom.
Aksayamati said: "Yes, Śāriputra!
The mental abidings (smṛtyupasthāna) of a bodhisattva are likewise inexhaustible."

He observes his own body and the bodies of others; he observes how the original actions of the body result in the karma of diligence, and examines how the retribution of the body is formed through various conditions. He knows that the body has no master and nothing within it to be craved.
It is just as when one observes external grasses, trees, various fruits, groves, and weeds, which all arise from causes and conditions and possess no name of a master;
this body is likewise like grass, trees, walls, tiles, stones, or a reflection in water, deluded by the five aggregates, the four great elements, and the sense bases.
Contemplate that one's own body is empty, devoid of a self, incapable of lasting long, and lacking solidity.
It is a fragile thing subject to separation; for this reason, one should not conceive of the body as "mine."
With this fragile body, which lacks any solidity, one should seek the essential meaning.
What is meant by "essential"?
It is said that the body of the Tathāgata is the true essence.
I shall diligently seek to attain the Buddha’s holy body, the infinite Dharma-body, which is indestructible like a diamond and transcends all mundane bodies within the three realms.

Even though this body may have immeasurable defects, one should, by means of it, eliminate all defilements and attain the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of emptiness. Through the power of diligent cultivation, one gathers a multitude of virtues; with sincerity, one examines the body composed of the four great elements, resolving that this very body shall be dedicated to seeking the Way for the sake of all sentient beings.

Just as one observes the four external elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—which form various shapes such as gates, wells, stoves, houses, and the means of livelihood to provide security for the masses;

so too is my body composed of the four elements. It relies upon various things and produces various and immeasurable resources, whereby one attains the activity of maintaining and nourishing the body.

"Contemplate that the suffering of the body is beyond measure; contemplate that the physical form is impermanent and that one undergoes the cycle of birth and death, coming and going. One should no longer greedily crave the infinite reception of a physical form.

Contemplate that the body is without self, yet the various classes of sentient beings do not understand its beginning and end; you should instruct and admonish them so that they grow weary of and loathe this."

Contemplate the body as tranquil; when about to enter a state of meditative concentration, practice stillness and silence. One should contemplate the emptiness of the body—free from conceptualization and free from aspiration—and thus return to the fundamental limit of profound serenity and purity.
"He observes his own body and observes the bodies of others; he finds no cause for attachment or delight, does not reckon them as solid or firm, and knows they do not endure.
He examines the activities of his internal body and no longer follows after the afflictions of the internal defilements or the calamities of craving and desire;
furthermore, observing the external body, he never again unites it with external objects."
The body is free from toil and defilement, and its conduct is pure;
once the body is purified, one subsequently attains the excellence of physical marks and a majestic form.

When the physical form is thus perfected, one surpasses all devas and worldly humans, with a countenance so sublime that it has no peer. This is the bodhisattva’s establishment of the foundations of mindfulness by observing his own body and observing the bodies of others.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva observing their own sensations and observing the sensations of others to attain the stillness of mind?
A bodhisattva resolves to observe in this way: that all which is experienced is nothing but suffering."

He examines sensations and seeks after noble wisdom; he selects clear intelligence and yearns for tranquility. Even when encountering pleasure, he is not bound by desire, for if one exists within desire, it leads to suffering.
Seeing all sentient beings fallen into the various evil destinies and the hardships of the three miserable realms, he gives rise to great compassion; yet he is not bound by the net of fetters.
Although his body encounters neither suffering nor pleasure, but various sensations of pain and itchiness, he is not bound by the net of the darkness of ignorance.

Although they abide in feelings, their minds remain in tranquil concentration; regarding the suffering or pleasure they have experienced since beginningless time, they manifest to sentient beings through noble wisdom that these feelings are of no benefit, thereby causing them to cast them aside and eliminate all suffering and pleasure for all sentient beings.
Donning the armor of detachment, he thought to himself:

"These multitudes of beings remain submerged in sensations that they do not recognize; they are bound to the ground of manifold sufferings and sensations, constantly harboring grief and sorrow. They rely upon the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant and thereby become deluded and bewildered; for this reason, they do not enter into wisdom."

The one who embraces great compassion enters into wisdom and thoroughly understands the cessation of all sensations of pain; through this great compassion, he causes all sentient beings to be freed from various hardships and proclaims the sūtras for their sake.
"What is meant by 'feeling' (vedanā)?
It is when the mind harbors affliction or experiences pleasure.
What is meant by 'selecting this absence of feeling'?"
There is no self, no person, and no life-span; furthermore, that bodhisattva does not rely upon sensation, nor is there any craving or guarding.

The sensations he experiences are without repetitive activity and without inverted sensation; they are also free from the sensations of false imaginings and various views, and free from the sensations of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the sensations of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
That which belongs to the eye arises from causes and conditions; calculating it as suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—this is called sensation (*vedanā*).
To state the essential point: the same applies internally and externally; arising from causes and conditions, it results in sensation.

Regarding suffering, pleasure, good, evil, and that which is neither painful nor pleasant, the causes of these sensations are tenfold: First, the cause of sensation is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Second, as for sensation, it is said to exist internally and externally.

Third, as for sensation, it follows past teachings, proceeds from future actions, and is caused by present consciousness. Fourth, as for sensation, it arises from the four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind. Fifth, as for sensation, it arises from mindfulness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Sixth, as for sensation, it arises because of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Seventh, as for sensation, it arises because of the seven types of consciousness. Eighth, as for sensation, it arises from the eightfold wrong path (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*), due to delusion and confusion. Ninth, as for sensation, it refers to the nine abodes of spirits (*navāyatana*). Tenth, as for sensation, it refers to the ten unwholesome karmas (*daśākuśala-karma*)."

To state the essential point: all sensations of pain and pleasure arise from the craving for enjoyment; because they result from the pursuit of desire, it is said that the number of such people is incalculable and their suffering is immeasurable.

"A Bodhisattva observes his own sensations and observes the sensations of others; knowing that the various multitudes give rise to differentiated sensations, he should manifest the work of wisdom so that all sentient beings, through the wisdom regarding sensations, may perceive the roots of virtue and eliminate all transgressions. This is the Bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to the sensations of himself and others."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva observing his own mind and observing the minds of others as the application of mindfulness?

It is that the bodhisattva’s mind is never negligent or forgetful; in every movement and step, he constantly guards himself and further examines it. As soon as a thought arises, it is immediately extinguished and has no place of permanent abiding; it does not abide within, nor does it abide without, nor is it found between the two."

Since I first gave rise to the bodhicitta, that mind has been utterly extinguished; it has departed, dispersed, and is entirely without location. That which is non-existent and without location cannot be localized.

Wherever the mind may dwell, the root of all the various virtues accumulated by that mind likewise undergoes cessation, separation, and dispersal; it abides nowhere and cannot be differentiated. That which serves as the cause for inspiring the aspiration for the Way is also naturally so. For this reason, it is said: the mind does not know the mind, the mind does not see the mind, and mind and mind do not depend upon one another.
"What is meant by 'arousing the mind for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment and attaining supreme, right awakening'?

As for that path-mind, it does not unite with [ordinary] goodness; that fundamental mind of goodness does not conjoin with a mind of encouragement or assistance; and that pure mind does not abandon the path-mind. When a person contemplates this, they are neither afraid, nor terrified, nor do they harbor any dread."

Furthermore, he reflects that the twelve links of dependent origination are exceedingly profound and subtle; they do not fail to produce the fruits sown through the law of retribution, yet the mind does not cling to any phenomena whatsoever.

If causes and conditions arise from karmic retribution, and all dharmas possess neither ultimate truth nor a sovereign ruler, such that beings act according to their whims and delude themselves, I shall apply myself with diligence, maintaining single-mindedness so that it does not waver.
"What is meant by mental phenomena?
What is meant by delusion?
The mind is like a magical illusion; there is nothing that can purify it—this is what is meant by mental phenomena."
Even if one were to relinquish everything, to understand the nature of delusion and to encourage the establishment of a Buddha-land—this too is delusion.
When the mind is like a dream from which one has awakened and no longer knows its location, this is the nature of the mind;
if, within the observance of the precepts, one practices with vigilance and then encourages oneself toward these five supernormal powers, this is transformation.
The mind is like a wild horse; its beginning and end are utterly extinguished—this is the nature of the mind.

If, by means of the power of patience that accords with all things, one pacifies and harmonizes it, adorning the mind with perfect awakening and transforming it, employing this to provide encouragement and assistance—this is called transformation.
The mind is like the moon in water, ultimately and naturally tranquil and serene; this is the nature of the mind.
If one exerts all diligence to inspire and bring to fulfillment the countless Buddha-dharmas, this is transformative manifestation.
That the mind cannot be grasped and cannot be seen is the nature of the mind;

furthermore, to be fully equipped with meditative reflection, the doors of liberation, samādhi, and right reception, as well as the Buddha’s concentration and intention, constitutes transformative manifestation.
“The mind is formless, incomparable, beyond instruction, and without material appearance; this is the nature of the mind.
If one can proclaim and discern wisdom, assist in the Buddha-way, and investigate past ages, this constitutes transformative manifestation.”
That the mind does not arise at all in the absence of causes and conditions is the nature of the mind;
that it can guide and direct all roots of virtue is its transformative power.
That the mind ultimately does not arise when there is no object of opposition is the nature of the mind.
If one cultivates the mind of the Way based on causes, dharmas, or retributions, this is called "transformation.
When the sphere of that mind is forever free from defilement and turbidity, and is originally unarisen, this is the "dharma of the mind.
If one guides and governs the mind so as to attain retribution and reach the Buddha-realm, this is called "transformation."

"The Bodhisattva observes his own mind and observes the minds of others; having attained supernormal powers, his mind becomes concentrated, and he immediately perceives the mental activities of all sentient beings, whereby he explains that both transgressions and blessings are all spontaneous."

When a bodhisattva perceives their own mind and perceives the minds of others, they give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Having given rise to great compassion, they transform sentient beings without weariness.
Their mind is neither extinguished nor exhausted; they remain steadfastly established in that mind, not becoming defiled by the common dusts of birth and death.

Being able to self-restrain the mind, by means of this noble wisdom and penetrating mind, one enters into the state of non-arising and non-production; one does not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but constantly governs the mind so as to be capable of fulfilling all the dharmas of the Buddha-way. In a single moment of thought, through the mind of wisdom, one attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path as the Most Perfectly Awakened One. This is what is meant by a Bodhisattva examining his own mind and observing the minds of others to attain the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"What is meant by a bodhisattva observing their own dharmas and observing the dharmas of others to attain the application of mindfulness to dharmas?
It is to see all dharmas universally with the eye of clear wisdom, never forgetting them until the attainment of the Buddha-way."

Observing their own dharmas and observing the dharmas of others, at that time the Bodhisattva perceives all dharmas; through the perception of emptiness, they bring about liberation from the meaning of emptiness, liberation from the signless, and the fulfillment of the wishless, whereby they transcend all arising and are free from all conditioned formations.

Equally perceiving all phenomena and relinquishing the twelvefold chain of dependent origination, the bodhisattva contemplates the activity of the dharma-realm; observing phenomena, they do not follow what is non-dharmic, nor do they calculate a self, a person, a life-span, or a location—this is called "the Dharma."
What is called "unrighteousness" (adharma)?

It is to perceive a self, to calculate the existence of persons and lifespans, to view things as subject to annihilation, to reckon that there is something eternally enduring, and to perceive the phenomena of union and dispersion regarding existence and non-existence.
"All dharmas are indeed dharmas, yet all dharmas are also non-dharmas.
Why is this? Because one who understands the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) finds that all these dharmas are in accord with the Dharma."
"Self-conceptually calculating 'I' and 'mine,' one is bound by various views; thus, all these dharmas are entirely non-dharmas.
He observes his own dharmas and observes the dharmas of others; when a bodhisattva practices this, he does not perceive any dharmas.
What is the Buddha-dharma?
What is not the Buddha-dharma?
That which has no path, no liberation, and no birth-and-death—this is that which can guide and illuminate all dharmas.
Abiding among sentient beings, he attains the unobstructed and infinite great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and having healed all their afflictions (*kleśa*), his own mind gives rise to this thought:
"This is neither free from dust and desire, nor is it not free from dust and desire."

Why is this so? Because that which is the destination is the liberation through equality; one does not doubt the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor fear desire. One who thoroughly understands this is called a Buddha.

Defilements and desires are spontaneous, and the Way is also spontaneous. When one establishes the mind in this manner, although there is that which dwells, there is no fixed location; it is called "dwelling" because it does not dwell upon the intention to dwell—this is what is meant by dwelling.
“Abiding in the dharma-realm, yet not abiding in the dharma-realm and not abiding in the realm of persons—this state of non-abiding is called ‘space. All dharmas are equal to space.”
If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the dharmas of their own body and contemplates the dharmas of others, they will be able to guide and lead them toward the dharmas of the Buddhas' path.
All dharmas ultimately converge in the dharma of liberation; one who understands this is then able to manifest it, exhausting the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) yet exhausting nothing at all.
The Way has no place of arising and no place where it is not born; one observes sentient beings without ever abandoning the primordial limit of non-arising.

One proceeds toward the mental abiding in phenomena, fixing the mind upon all dharmas so that they remain steadfastly established, without attachment to the teachings of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
What is meant by non-attachment?
What is meant by abiding in the proper place?

It is when the mind, wherever it may be, is always able to remain steadfast; its dwelling is not deluded, and it never forgets. Having observed the ultimate limit of where these phenomena originate, one also observes other phenomena and thereby attains the stilling of the mind.

To proclaim immeasurable chapters and phrases, to practice boundlessly in accordance with the Buddha-dharma, to gladden the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings, to subdue all Māras and attain sovereign wisdom—this is what is called the meaning of the Way.
This is how a bodhisattva, by observing their own phenomena and the phenomena of others, attains the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
What are the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*) that are inexhaustible?

Regarding all unwholesome phenomena of the body that have not yet arisen, one ensures they do not arise; regarding those already arisen, one seeks to extinguish them and cultivates diligence. One restrains the mind so that its thoughts accord with the meaning [of the Dharma], increasing one's diligent effort further. This is called the practice of equanimity in the observance of diligent conduct.
This refers to not losing the proper sequence, practicing equanimity, and being able to restrain the mind to contemplate the true truths.
Why is this so? Because when one’s thoughts accord with the meaning [of the Dharma], unwholesome and evil states no longer recur.
"What is called unwholesome?
It is the violation of precepts, the disturbance of concentration, and the delusion of wisdom.
What is called the violation of precepts?"
To wish to be born in the heavens while claiming to have violated the precepts—
disobeying the teachings of the Dharma and being deficient in the categories of the precepts— is what is meant by violating the precepts.
What is meant by "disturbing meditative concentration"?
To violate propriety and decorum, to practice without single-minded dedication, and for the mind to dwell on other thoughts—this is to disturb meditative concentration.
What is meant by being deluded regarding wisdom?
To sever all false views, to perceive various categories, and to encounter inverted matters and obstructive dharmas (āvaraṇa)—such deficiencies in wisdom are called unwholesome.
If various evils and such-like dharmas arise and one does not tolerate them, this is decisiveness of mind.

If various evil and unwholesome dharmas arise, one immediately recognizes them; knowing they are contrary to the Dharma and result in unwholesome retribution, and understanding that they cause depletion and constitute defiled conduct.
To enter the dark chamber and cultivate the practice of accordant righteousness to eliminate impure desires;

to employ a mind of loving-kindness to remove hatred; and to understand the twelve links of dependent origination to extinguish ignorance—exhausting all such defilements is what is called "severance."

Arising from identical causes and conditions, one contemplates that which is produced as having neither beginning nor end and thus nothing to be severed; all phenomena result from habitual practice—this is the second abandonment of intention (*saṃkalpa-prahāṇa*).

"Even if wholesome dharmas have not yet arisen, one should encourage them to arise; one should manifest diligence so that they may restrain their own minds, and praise their immeasurable virtues. Why is this so? [Because...]"
The wholesome dharmas are immeasurable, and those which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice require that one take delight in the faculty of wisdom.
Since the root of all virtues is brought about through diligence, which manifests and leads to the source of meritorious blessings—this is the third right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*).

"What may be called such: when wholesome dharmas arise, one causes them to remain firm; one does not fear losing their integrity nor neglects them; one increasingly delights in the fundamental source, practicing with diligence day and night, and restraining one's own mind to encourage and assist the Path—this is called equanimity."
Why is this? Because the root of merit for one who encourages the aspiration for the Way is imperishable. Why is this?
Their mind is pure; though they dwell within the triple world, they have no attachments.
If there is exhortation or assistance, if their virtue relies upon the triple world, it is said to be exhausted;

if they can exhort and delight in setting their will upon all-knowledge, this is called the root of universal wisdom that is never diminished or depleted—this is the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*).
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing the bases of psychic power?
There are four bases of psychic power; having already aroused oneself with joy and diligent perseverance, by what practice does one bring forth the foundations of the bases of psychic power?"

One should practice the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and should always cultivate the four states of non-negligence, expanding one's mind without craving for the body.

By being able to discipline the mind, one honors the first dhyāna; proceeding thus through to the fourth, one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) such that the body and mind become light and agile. Once the body and mind are thus made agile, this is called entering the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); by entering these supernormal powers, one gives rise to the power of the spiritual bases (*ṛddhipāda*).

“Diligently cultivating vigor and fundamentally setting one’s will upon the Path, because of delighting in diligence, one immediately draws near to the meaning of the Path; because of vigor, one is able to accomplish this Dharma; because of diligent cultivation, one attains this principle. By observing with a single mind and through skillful means, one brings forth supernormal powers; therefore, it is called the ‘basis of supernormal power’ (ṛddhipāda).”

Because one constantly delights in it, one is able to undergo transformation; because of diligence, one is able to bring it to fulfillment; because of single-minded devotion, one is able to comprehend the vast. Thus, by briefly cultivating virtue for oneself, one immediately accomplishes the Way.

There are those who, by means of the bodhisattva’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), attain proximity through this very cause; they possess mastery over the mind such that wherever they wish to go, nothing can obstruct them.

Having attained the ultimate source through the practice of the truths and being fully perfected in all practices, he cannot be restrained by Māra; he is equal to empty space, seeing boundlessly, hearing without limit, with infinite concentration of mind and bottomless supernormal power. He perceives all faculties and beholds their very origin; this is the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible practice of the four bases of supernormal power.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the five faculties (pañcendriya) that is inexhaustible?

What are these five? First is the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya); second is the faculty of diligence (vīryendriya); third is the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya); fourth is the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya); and fifth is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya)."
"What is called the faculty of faith?
It is to always have faith in all dharmas.
What is meant by 'dharmas'?"

As for right view, it is to have faith while wandering through birth and death, following one’s spiritual capacity to accomplish those practices; not delighting in other deities, but understanding the meaning of the supreme First Truth and being liberated from the profound and subtle twelve links of dependent origination; being without self or person, empty, signless, and wishless, free from the marks of attachment; universally believing in all phenomena without falling into various views; believing in all Buddha-dharmas and in the ten powers and four fearlessnesses; harboring neither doubt nor hesitation; and gathering together the Buddha-dharmas so as to make them limitless—this is called the faculty of faith.
"What is called the faculty of diligence?

It is that by means of this diligence regarding the dharmas one has faith in, the various faculties become increasingly clear, surpassing the light of the sun and moon; this is the faculty of diligence."
"The dharma by which one cultivates the faculty of diligence is such that, for this reason, the faculty of mind is not lost.
That mind is vast and does not abide in any extreme; this is called the faculty of mind."

"When the mind is thus tranquil and does not conflict with the faculty of mind (*manas*), and the mind is as vast as space, employing this faculty of mind with single-minded concentration and without distraction—this is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
When that faculty of concentration remains constantly in the state of quiescence and maintains exclusive focus on the One—this is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
To observe and clearly understand, such that one discriminates within these phenomena and their forms as being without self (*anātman*)—this is called the faculty of wisdom."
"One who can fulfill these five faculties possesses all the Buddha-dharmas; such a fulfiller dwells in the stage of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) without wavering.
It is like those of external paths or seers possessing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), who, though they may look into a womb, cannot yet distinguish in advance the male or female faculty."

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise: as long as the bodhisattva’s training in the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) is not yet perfected, they do not bestow the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); only when the five faculties have been fully mastered do they receive the prediction. This is what is meant by the inexhaustibility of the bodhisattva’s five faculties.
"What are the powers?
There are five powers that are inexhaustible.
What are these five?"
First is the power of faith; second is the power of diligence; third is the power of intention; fourth is the power of concentration; and fifth is the power of wisdom.
"What is called the power of faith?

It is to always maintain a sincere mind, remaining in solitary stillness without becoming confused or distracted; though there are no physical forms, one dwells in the vision of the Buddha’s form, and likewise knows the teachings of others with a single-minded tranquility. Wherever this power of faith abides, it never regresses; this is called the power of faith."
"What is called the power of diligence? It is to constantly and fundamentally cultivate diligence;

wherever one cultivates virtue, one is industrious regarding the scriptures. In every place where one is born, the mind is firm and strong. The roots of virtue thus cultivated cannot be destroyed by anyone in the heavens or the world, nor can they be restrained so as not to increase. Because of this, the roots of virtue flourish and reach the limitlessness of the infinite—this is the power of diligence."
"What is meant by the power of the mind?

It is when one dwells upon the Dharma with a mind that is neither lax nor remiss; such that the various afflictions of craving and desire are unable to transgress it, and by this power of the mind, one transcends all worldly defilements."
As for that bodhisattva, whatever the mind intends, nothing in the heavens or the world can disturb it; this is called the power of the mind (*cittabala*).
What is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*)?
Whether in a great assembly or amidst the clamor of a crowd, one remains in a state of tranquility wherever one is, proclaiming the power of the Way through every movement and step.
In the first dhyāna, there is nothing that can obscure or obstruct; the roots of virtue cultivated therein and the dedicated practice of the Path likewise cannot be destroyed.
In the second dhyāna, one cultivates joy; internally pure and serene, it is free from obstruction.
In the third dhyāna, one desires to transform sentient beings and protect the True Dharma without [discursive] observation.
Even when reaching the fourth dhyāna, there is likewise no obstruction.

Because one cultivates the categories of meditation through these four dhyānas such that none can surpass them, and because the concentrated mind cultivated therein cannot be disturbed, this mastery over the concentrated mind is called the power of concentration (samādhi-bala).
"What is called the power of wisdom?

Whether regarding mundane dharmas or supramundane dharmas, one is able to fully comprehend all places where they arise; there is no one who can act as one's teacher. One thoroughly knows worldly chapters, phrases, characters, and the karmic deeds established therein—divine arts, the Five Classics, the Six Arts, and various secular books. Without studying them, the Bodhisattva naturally knows them, as well as all supramundane dharmas, reaching complete mastery in everything."

By means of this sagely and luminous wisdom-mind, the bodhisattva is able to penetrate all things; he walks alone and without peer throughout the heavens and the world, proclaiming the teachings according to the occasion. This is called the inexhaustible power of wisdom.
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Six;
The Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
"What is meant by the factors of enlightenment? There are seven factors of enlightenment practiced by a bodhisattva.

What are the seven? First is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; second is the factor of enlightenment of dharma-investigation; third is the factor of enlightenment of vigor; fourth is the factor of enlightenment of joy; fifth is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; sixth is the factor of enlightenment of concentration; and seventh is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity."
"What is meant by the awakening of the mind?

It is when one contemplates the teachings that have been reflected upon, examines them according to the authentic scriptures, reflects upon the principles of the sutras, extols them with focused mindfulness, and observes one's own mind; thus, being unable to grasp at the characteristics of phenomena, one is able to understand this."
What is meant by "all phenomena are without marks"?
Their marks are spontaneous, and all phenomena are entirely empty.
To be able to clearly comprehend such awakened awareness is called the "mind that awakens the mind."
"What is called the awakening-factor of dharma?
It is when one can discern the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the sūtra-dharma, selecting those dharmas that accord with the meaning of the treasuries;
and if they do not accord with the treasuries, returning them to the correct meaning."
If there is no ultimate meaning, there would be no proximate meaning, remote meaning, pure meaning, or profound meaning.
If one thoroughly understands the power of the Dharma through the primary meaning, one will discern that which is combined, that which is dispersed, and that which is either resolved or unresolved.
To be able to discern all things and know their origins and endings—this is called the awakening factor of dharma (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If one employs this mind to proclaim the Dharma, embracing faith, concentration, and the protected noble wisdom; through subtle power, delighting in firm mindfulness that cannot be obstructed or diverted; and diligently practicing this balanced conduct—this is the awakening factor of energy.
"What is meant by the awakening factor of joy?

It is when one has firm faith and does not abandon those dharmas that are cherished and delightful; one constantly harbors joy and is free from timidity; body, speech, and mind are always at rest; and one contemplates and applies oneself to the Dharma, thereby digesting the afflictions of worldly toil and the suffering of desire. This is called the awakening factor of joy."
"What is meant by the awakening factor of faith?

If one can forever distance oneself from the body and mind, from craving, desire, and worldly afflictions regarding that which is believed, and the mind abides in concentrated intent, this is called the awakening factor of faith."
"What is meant by the awakening factor of concentration?

It is by means of mental concentration that one penetrates and realizes all phenomena; through the discernment of noble wisdom, the mind is applied with diligence, clearly cognizing all phenomena so that the faculties become sharp and penetrating. One severs all inverted views and dwells nowhere; it is solely through concentration that one is able to achieve this."
To understand that there is no self and that all phenomena are equal is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the awakening factor of vigilance (*apramāda-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If one can contemplate and discern the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), such that the mind does not race about nor dwell upon worldly dharmas; if the mind is boundless and is not deluded by worldly dharmas; if it does not abide in provisional designations and nothing can move it; and if it is without volition, without thought, without joy, and without grief—for these reasons, one attains the Path of the Sages.
The patient acceptance of the dharma in accordance with reality is called the awakening factor of vigilance.
These seven factors of awakening are inexhaustible.
What is right view?

The noble sages who transcend the world do not dwell in the notion of a self, nor do they dwell in the notions of a person or a life-span; they have no reliance on views, they do not dwell in the view of existence or the view of non-existence, they do not dwell in the roots of merit, and they do not fall into false views or the sixty-two kinds of doubt—this is called right view.

"What is right mindfulness? The ordinary person is mindful of the afflictions of lust, anger, and delusion, as well as the defilements of worldly toil. The Bodhisattva practitioner does not think of these; they think only of the categories manifested by the matters of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. They constantly mind the meaning of the Path, always making their will one-pointed—meaning that the mind is not deviant. This is called right mindfulness."
"What is called right speech?

It refers to the words spoken without regarding oneself or others; the language is gentle and does not expound coarse meanings. Using this to proclaim the teaching and enter the Noble Path, one refrains from worldly chatter and useless talk—this is called right speech."
"What is meant by 'right governance' (samyak-nīti)?

As for those who practice, they do not engage in the various matters of transgression or merit; rather, they cultivate only the principle of the Middle Way and equanimity—this is called right governance."

"What is called right action? It is to employ the words of the noble ones so as to bring great joy, while knowing contentment; not abandoning moderation, not coveting gain or offerings, not harboring flattery or deceit, and keeping the mind from wandering; whatever one cultivates, one immediately maintains through skillful care of one's deportment; seeing others receive offerings, one harbors no envy; regarding the sustenance one receives for oneself, one does so merely to maintain the body; one does not commit transgressions, but follows the Buddha’s teachings and instructions—this is called right action."
"What is meant by right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*)?

If one cultivates skillful means in accordance with the true teaching, and does not follow lust, anger, delusion, or craving to become defiled by the dust of the world; if one always remains far removed from these [defilements], delights in the Noble Path, and attains the meaning of cessation and the unconditioned (*nirvāṇa*); if one constantly contemplates this—this is called right effort."
"What is meant by right intention?

It is when the mind abides in truthfulness and sincerity, free from attachment and devoid of flattery; it perceives fully the hardships of birth and death, contemplates the Way of the Unconditioned with a single mind, and does not forget the path of the Sages—this is called right intention."
"What is called right concentration?
Because the mind is concentrated, it is termed equanimity; for this reason, all phenomena are entirely equal, and one establishes equanimity within right concentration."
If there are bodhisattvas who abide in this samādhi, they deliver sentient beings equally without overstepping right wisdom; this is called right concentration that is inexhaustible.

"The Buddhas of the past, future, and present all travel this path; if there are bodhisattvas who follow and train in this teaching and proclaim it, this is called the Eightfold Path that is inexhaustible."
Aksayamati said: "Yes, Śāriputra!
The bodhisattva is tranquil, and that which he observes is likewise inexhaustible."

What is meant by "tranquility"? It is when the mind is serene, secluded, and steadfast; when the sensory faculties are not distracted, remaining focused and free from discursive thought; when one's nature is peaceful, neither precipitate nor violent; when one reflects with measured composure, relinquishing unwholesome thoughts; when one delights in the singular truth, eliminates all clamor and bustle, and finds joy in solitude; when the body is secluded and the mind is never disturbed, contemplating dwelling in seclusion.

He is free from all evils and does not conceal his faults; he does not fall into wrong views and knows contentment. His disposition is pure and his deportment is complete; he does not transgress the rules of propriety and knows how to act according to the times. His movements are appropriate, and he makes offerings in accordance with the teachings. He gathers the power of virtue without being self-important, and while his merits are far-renowned, he does not rely on fame.

With a mind focused and dedicated, he delights in solitude; with single-mindedness, he practices meditative reflection, giving rise to loving-kindness and compassion while practicing sympathetic joy, and upholding protective equanimity. From the first dhyāna up to the eight gates of inconceivable concentration, this is called tranquility.
Furthermore, its state of stillness and its activity are immeasurable; if one can thoroughly penetrate this activity, it is called "stillness.
What is meant by "contemplation"?

It is the discernment of wisdom and the cultivation of the path of Dharma, [realizing] there is no self and no person, no life-span and no vital principle. One contemplates the body of the five aggregates and the elements of the four great dharmas; one contemplates the various sense bases (*āyatana*) as being like an empty village, discerning their complete formation and observing them with knowledge.

Following the twelve links of dependent origination without confusion, they abandon all views; beholding the fruits of retribution resulting from causes and conditions, they clearly understand the fruits of virtue. Having realized and witnessed this, they enter into the true and correct state, and being able to enter therein, they contemplate the wisdom of the various sages.

"What is called 'contemplation' refers to the illumination of the equal Dharma; therein one correctly and truly contemplates all phenomena and perceives no distinct dharmas. Being empty, signless, and wishless, one beholds only these three gates of liberation."

What is called "contemplation" means not perceiving a location, a house, or a dwelling; nor is it that one does not perceive the arising of phenomena, for one does not obtain the karma of inverted delusions.

What is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) is that wherein there is ultimately nothing seen; if there is nothing seen, this is called contemplation. To have no seeing amidst all that is seen—this is called contemplation.
One who sees in this way is said to possess the vision of ultimate truth; such a person is able to understand and follow the Buddha’s teaching.
One who sees in this way, for the sake of being a bodhisattva, neither falls into non-action nor abides in formal practice; this is called contemplation.
"This is what is called the Bodhisattva’s tranquil and correct contemplation, which is inexhaustible.
Akṣayamati said: "Yes, Śāriputra!"
The Bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī and eloquence are inexhaustible.
What is meant by "dhāraṇī"?

It refers to the accumulation of the roots of virtue, the contemplation of the great enterprise, and the upholding, reciting, and mindful retention of the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma; contemplating them, cherishing them, and never abandoning diligent effort—this is called dhāraṇī.

Furthermore, as for "dhāraṇī," it refers to the ability to receive and accept all that is spoken regarding the various dharmas; whether from śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the assembly of bodhisattvas, or all sentient beings, one is able to recognize and remember their phrasing, speech, and the principles they expound—this is called dhāraṇī.

Even if the kalpa were to burn, the heavens and earth were to meet with calamity, and his physical life were to come to an end—though that bodhisattva may encounter such hardships, he continues to maintain the *dhāraṇī* of consciousness within his heart, never forgetting it nor becoming confused or deluded. With the eye of noble wisdom, he perceives all phenomena as clearly as if examining the palm of his own hand; this is the *dhāraṇī*, which is likewise inexhaustible.
"What is meant by 'eloquence that is inexhaustible'? So-called eloquence refers to speech that is unimpeded.

When expounding upon principles, there is no one who can restrain it; its eloquence is so sharp and penetrating that none can sever it. Its vocal eloquence is without limit or interruption; when questioned suddenly, it responds immediately according to the occasion without difficulty. It is thoroughly penetrating like water, with not a single obstruction."

This eloquence has been attained through the retribution of pure conduct cultivated in past lives; it is protected by all Buddhas and guarded by all devas. What he expounds shall never be in vain; his words shall not be offensive, and he shall proceed toward the path of unconditioned nirvana.
Such eloquence as this is fully perfected; with reverence, diligence, and humility, he proclaims the Dharma after discerning the capacities of others.

Those who hear it each obtain what they could not have attained through their own prior reflection. To those who come to inquire, I shall speak of this; having entered the various assemblies, I observe the faculties of people and the mental inclinations of sentient beings, and thus preach the Dharma for them.

Having originally come forth to be born among humans, his resolve and nature are true and correct; he proclaims the sutras for an entire kalpa without ceasing, and the scriptures he expounds are free from all obstruction—this is the inexhaustible eloquence of a bodhisattva.
Akṣayamati said:
"Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who teach that all dharmas ultimately revert to impermanence and that no thing belongs to a self; the wisdom with which they speak is inexhaustible.
They proclaim that all is suffering and that all dharmas are without self; even as bodhisattvas, their proclamations of these truths are likewise inexhaustible."
What is meant by impermanence?
To observe that all matters, from their beginning to their end, ultimately revert to impermanence and possess no fixed law.
That which is impermanent cannot be made permanent; from the very beginning, there has been nothing that is not impermanent. This is the meaning of impermanence.
What is meant by the meaning of suffering?

Although there may be joy and pleasure, they must inevitably come to an end; such wishes do not endure for long. When one discusses the various sufferings, they all tend toward emptiness and non-existence.
That which is empty and non-existent is also void and lacks reality; the meaning of emptiness and the meaning of suffering are perfectly equal and no different.
What is meant by "non-body"?

Regarding the self, there is no self at all, neither in its beginning nor its end; that [self] is likewise empty, quiescent, and without essence. For those who conceive of emptiness and the meaning of emptiness, there is entirely no body.
What is meant by the meaning of tranquility?
To have no tranquility within tranquility is what is called tranquility; that which is liberated has no evenness even within equanimity—this is called tranquility.
What is called "liberation" refers to practicing silent stillness and eliminating all perceptions;
having eliminated all perceptions, this is termed the tranquility of unconditioned *nirvāṇa*. This is the meaning of "extinction."
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma of the Four Truths, which is inexhaustible.
"The path practiced by the bodhisattva is always the cultivation of the One Way, not following other practices.
What is meant by the Way of the One Vehicle?"
The Bodhisattva walks alone without a companion; by himself alone he attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One, donning the great armor of virtue.

Having personally gathered the power of supreme diligence, his body stands alone without following the teachings of others; transcending all worldly powers, he wanders by himself, clad in the firm armor of the non-permanent virtues. By means of this, he transforms and enlightens all sentient beings—this is called "teaching and transforming."
That which is taught and exhorted is the instruction of all the worthy sages; that which is taught and exhorted by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas is called "instruction and transformation.
Giving is not my companion, but I am the companion of giving;

likewise, upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are not my companions, but I am the companion of wisdom, yet I do not dwell even in these six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

I shall follow and practice the various *pāramitās* and the deeds of the four debts of gratitude (*catur-ṛṇa*), not giving rise to the thought, "I shall establish and encompass these four debts of gratitude.

To speak in brief: regarding all roots of wholesome virtue (*kuśala-mūla*), they cannot establish themselves; I shall establish and encompass all such roots of virtue. Such dharmas as these have no companion; they should stand independently, without a second partner.

Abiding in the adamantine field, he subdues all māras through the power of his own body; in the mere instant of a single thought, he attains the unexcelled, true, and correct path and becomes a Most Perfectly Awakened One. This is the Bodhisattva’s path of the Single Vehicle, which is inexhaustible.
Aksayamati said: "Yes, Śāriputra!
The skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) of a bodhisattva is likewise inexhaustible."
What is meant by skillful means (*upāya*)?

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, according to the timing and what is appropriate for each situation, encounter the teachings of the Way and bring about transformation; through skillful means, they draw near to the mind of the Way.
That which is skillful means arises from emptiness and has no limit; its nature and disposition adapt to the times, thereby bringing about extraordinary excellence.

Those who possess skillful means are able to fully perfect all the *pāramitās*; in whatever place they are born, they employ expedient means to practice precepts, generosity, and patience, guarding their body, speech, and mind, so as to reach the path of Buddhahood without ceasing their diligence. If one lacks skillful means, one will fail and lose that diligence.

With skillful means and a single mind, one advances toward noble wisdom; otherwise, the mind becomes distracted. Through skillful means and wisdom, one does not abandon the hardships of circulating through birth and death.

Skillful means and compassion provide protection for many and eliminate all that is unkind. Skillful means and pity do not weary of birth and death, but transform and enlighten all beings. Skillful means and joy do not delight in any objects of attachment or longing. Skillful means and protection cultivate the roots of myriad virtues without ever turning back.

Through skillful means, he attains the divine eye of a Buddha, with ten eyes that perceive the ten directions without limit; through skillful means, he attains the divine ear of a Buddha, with ten ears that hear the sounds of the ten directions and the mental activities and physical forms of beings; through skillful means, he knows the minds of others and perceives the faculties of sentient beings, fully understanding their origins and ends; through skillful means, he contemplates past events and perceives the principles of the three periods—past, future, and present; through skillful means, his supernormal powers reach everywhere without restriction, transforming and enlightening the masses throughout the ten directions.

With skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he knows the natures of sentient beings and accordingly entices them with expedients; with skillful means, he practices and understands the beginning, end, and ultimate origin of the characteristics of all people; through skillful means, he delivers those beyond this shore to the further shore; with skillful means, he enters the dust of the world to transform the masses from their desires, leading them across all defilements; with skillful means, he lowers the burden and removes the heavy calamities borne by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); with skillful means, his conduct is boundless and that which he proclaims cannot be fully recorded, using the finite to explain the infinite; with skillful means, he exhorts and transforms those of weak and inferior faculties, encouraging those who retreat so that they may expand toward the limitless.
“By means of skillful expedients, they know the proper seasons—when to increase or decrease, advance or retreat, and when to act out of season;
by means of skillful expedients, they lead beings from the right path onto deviant paths, and then transform those dwelling on deviant paths so that they enter the right path;
by means of skillful expedients, they can cause what is meager to become vast, and what is vast to become infinite.”
By means of skillful expedients, they exhort those who are contentious and discordant, as well as their companions who harbor mutual hatred, to achieve harmony;
by means of skillful expedients, they cause those belonging to the ranks of inferior practitioners and the Lesser Vehicle to abide in the subtle and wondrous;
and by means of skillful expedients, they attain extinction (nirvāṇa) only to re-enter the cycle of birth and death for the sake of saving these remaining people.
By means of skillful expedients, they untie all fetters and open the obstructed nets;
by means of skillful expedients, they are able to destroy the knots, while their resolve remains patient;
by means of skillful expedients, they always abide in tranquility without falling into extinction.
Through skillful means, they are able to fully understand and master all that is practiced, maintaining dignified conduct and etiquette without ever failing in proper ritual;
through skillful means, they observe all sentient beings without violating the precepts, always remaining in accord with the correct prohibitions;
through skillful means, they engage in gathering and attracting others without resorting to contention or dispute.
By means of skillful expedients, they cause the Dharma to flourish and proclaim it throughout the ten directions;
by means of skillful expedients, they walk alone through the three realms without suffering or distress;
by means of skillful expedients, they attain the gate of liberation and reach the state of non-action.
By means of skillful expedients, one discards unwholesome conduct; though remaining amidst it, one does not become defiled by its dust.
By means of skillful expedients, one associates with those who follow the Way, entering together without contravening their instructions.
Through excellent skillful expedients, one relinquishes non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and is able to enter the cycle of birth and death to rescue and liberate beings from all afflictions.
By means of skillful expedients, they enter the realm of Māra to illuminate the roots of all worldly afflictions and sensual desires;
