by means of skillful expedients, they reckon all things as being neither existent nor non-existent. This is called the inexhaustible skillful expedient practiced by Bodhisattvas for entering [the world].
Aksayamati said: "It is so, Śāriputra!
The eighty categories of bodhisattva practice are inexhaustible; all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, are born from these eighty inexhaustible dharmas."

When the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati preached this chapter on the Inexhaustibility of the Dharma-gate, seventy-eight thousand people who had not previously resolved their minds toward the Path all simultaneously gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment;
fifty-two thousand bodhisattvas immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The entire assembly took various flowers, diverse kinds of incense, and precious flower-canopies, using them to scatter as offerings over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, and Akṣayamati.
All bodhisattvas reverently honor and take refuge in this essential sūtra of the Infinite.
In the void, the devas played celestial music and raised their voices in praise, saying:
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, having accumulated the roots of virtue over incalculable kalpas, has personally attained perfect enlightenment and extensively delivers all beings."

Now, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati has extolled this sūtra and proclaimed its fundamental principles and details with inexhaustible meaning. If there is anyone who, upon hearing these essential points of this *Akṣaya-sūtra*, does not harbor doubt in their heart, but instead faithfully upholds, recites, and explains it to others, being devoted to the words of the Buddha, they too shall attain such merit and inexhaustible meaning.
The Buddha took his own inner robe and bestowed it upon Akṣayamati, and at that moment, he praised the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You have expounded this sutra most excellently."
"The Tathāgata has exhorted us to take his place in joy; the Buddhas currently residing throughout the sands of the ten directions likewise join in this praise.
At that time, Akṣayamati took the robe bestowed by the Buddha and placed it upon the crown of his head, saying in praise:

"This robe of the World-Honored One should be honored with the crown of my head and served day and night; for it is the garment worn by the Supreme Honored Ones, the immeasurable Buddhas, who provide protection to both the heavens and the world."
At that moment, from each of the ten directions, precious banners, precious canopies, and precious streamers spontaneously arrived, covering the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
From within these precious robes, canopies, banners, and streamers, the teaching was spontaneously proclaimed, and voices spoke, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
"Akṣayamati Bodhisattva!
It is excellent that you have spoken these words and are able to expound and proclaim this inexhaustible Dharma-gate; all the Buddhas of the ten directions join in praising it.
At that time, Śāriputra came forward and asked the Buddha:
“From where have these precious robes, precious canopies, and precious banners come, that they now produce this sound?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“These are the Tathāgatas who were previously transformed by the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati; he caused the various classes of sentient beings to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and each has now attained perfect enlightenment in the ten directions. These Tathāgatas have therefore sent these here to provide offerings and repay the kindness of the Righteous Man’s original virtue, to proclaim the chapters on the great assembly of vast deeds, and to offer worship to the scriptures; thus they cover him from above.”

At that time, the entire assembly, having witnessed these transformations and heard what the Buddha had spoken, felt even greater reverence for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati. They leaped for joy, exclaiming:

"We have attained a great benefit; it is due to the profound merit of our past lives that we have been able to meet the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, prostrate before him, and consult him on this teaching. The merit of hearing this Dharma is immeasurable."

If there were someone who heard the name of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, their merit would be beyond limit; how much more so for one who meets him face-to-face, takes refuge in him, and hears this sutra?
That Buddha, the Great Sage, praises and encourages such a person—how much more so should he encourage an ordinary person!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If sons or daughters of good family who study the Bodhisattva vehicle were to dwell with all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, for an entire kalpa, making offerings and giving away everything they possess; if they were to uphold the prohibitions and precepts without any violation; if they were to endure all the pain and harm inflicted upon them by others; if they were to practice with fundamental vigor as if their heads were on fire; if they were to contemplate with single-mindedness without harboring confusion; and if they were to observe wisdom without missing its proper timing—revering and honoring the Buddhas in this manner until the end of the kalpa."

Furthermore, there may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who, upon hearing this sutra, believe it with deep sincerity, accept and uphold it, recite and read it, and practice it with single-minded devotion. With their progress and retreat governed by their own minds, the Buddha praises them, saying that they have fully perfected all six pāramitās and will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of supreme enlightenment.
Why is this? If there is a bodhisattva who studies this sutra, they will naturally give rise to this thought:
"I study this sutra so that I may fully explain and proclaim it everywhere for others."
"This is what is called being fully endowed with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Why is this so?
Because one who receives this sutra considers it the highest among all forms of giving—the gift of the Dharma—and draws near to the path of the Buddha."

If one is fully endowed with the prohibitive precepts, such that there is no transgression or debt in the perfection of restraint, and all practices are complete without a single deficiency or omission, it is therefore called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

Why is this? When a bodhisattva proclaims this sutra, they are universally endowed with the prohibitions and precepts; no sentient beings can fully describe them, nor can the merit of their achievements be attained by others.

Even if a bodhisattva endures all dharmas and remains unmoved in mind despite the harms and afflictions inflicted by the multitude, it is not as good as reciting and studying this essential sūtra and explaining it fully for others, thereby attaining the perfection of patience through the wisdom of practice.
To constantly practice diligence in body, speech, and mind, desiring to deliver all beings without ever becoming weary or indolent—this is called the Perfection of Diligence (Vīrya-pāramitā).
To be single-mindedly devoted to this sutra, contemplating it without distraction with a concentrated and focused mind—this is the Perfection of Meditation (Dhyāna-pāramitā) of the First Dhyāna.
If one examines the wisdom within this sutra in the present, grasping its meaning and knowing the direction toward which practice leads—this is called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñā-pāramitā).
"Yes, Śāriputra! If there are those who study this sūtra with diligence, even through limited practice they will fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva.
For this reason, you should form this contemplation: "

If there is a bodhisattva who takes up this sutra and recites it in their heart, or records it upon bamboo or silk to place it within a scroll, they have thereby grasped all dharmas and the scriptures of all Buddhas and held them in the palm of their hand; even if the four great elements were to transform and alter them, none could exert power to change their resolve for the Way.
Why is this? This sutra is named "The Seal of All Bodhisattvas. One should seek this seal; for if anyone upholds this seal, they will be able to follow and honor all the Buddha-dharmas.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues, all set aside their weapons to one side, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha:

“We four heavenly kings are disciples of the Buddha; having attained the fruits of the Path, we are able to provide protection and service for these sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, recite, and chant this sutra, honoring them as we would the Buddha.”
"Why is this? Because all vehicles arise from this.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have received and studied hundreds of thousands of sutras from the Tathāgata, yet I have never before heard the meaning of such a sutra as this, which elucidates the profound principles so thoroughly that no doubt remains."
In the past, when I was among the Trāyastriṃśa devas, I heard this sutra on many occasions, yet I had never before encountered such a teaching as this.

If there be any commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, provinces, cities, or great states where this sutra is proclaimed, one should go to those places to listen to it and consult upon its exposition; one should protect the Dharma Master, augmenting his vital strength, making his diligence firm and steadfast, ensuring he is courageous and undaunted, and that his eloquence is penetrating and sharp so that he may walk alone without fear.
"This son of good family, through his fearlessness, shall widely proclaim this sutra whether he is alone among the assembly or in a secluded place.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Kauśika!
If you rouse a courageous mind to protect the Dharma Master, you will delight in ensuring his vigor and diligence remain free from hindrance.
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! If one protects the Dharma Master, one protects the scriptures; by protecting the scriptures, one is able to protect and sustain all sentient beings.
At that time, the Brahma King Kṣāntivādin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I shall relinquish the bliss of the Brahma-heaven and my meditative states of mind, go to where the Dharma-preacher speaks the sutra to protect him, and manifest four auspicious omens so that he may be aware of them:
'The Brahma King has come to this assembly, followed by all the devas and humans.'"

"What are these four? First, causing them to see subtle and wondrous light; second, enabling them to smell celestial fragrances; third, the Dharma Master’s exposition being fluent and free from obstruction; fourth, the chapters and phrases following one another in sequence so that their meanings do not overlap. These are called the four matters."

When this sutra was being preached, his mind forgot nothing, his speech was eloquent and wise, and although the entire assembly desired to come and test him, none were able to disturb him; with minds mindful of the Dharma, they listened to the sutra with single-minded concentration. By means of these four qualities manifested through his wisdom, one should know that Brahmā and his retinue had come to that assembly.
Then Māra Pāpīyas came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Because of this sutra, I have been rendered weak and inferior, devoid of even a single shred of power. If there are bodhisattvas who hear this sutra, they shall receive a prediction of their future enlightenment, and the lands in which they travel shall regard them as Buddhas.”
"So be it, World-Honored One!
Having now witnessed the majestic power and holy strength of Akṣayamati, I have cast aside all arrogance and harbor no conceit. Why is this? Because—"

By means of this sutra, we shall provide protection, guardianship, and defense for the Dharma-preachers; from this day forth, we shall restrain ourselves and dare not disobey your instructions. Wherever this sutra is circulated and practiced, we shall nurture it from afar and dare not cause it disturbance or confusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should diligently receive this sutra, uphold it, recite it, read it, and explain it to others, so that the True Dharma may endure forever."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
I have already received and accepted it, and my recitation has reached mastery; yet I am not able to cause it to spread universally as the bodhisattvas do."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Be silent for now; there will naturally be those who shall cause it to be widely disseminated.
Within this assembly, there are bodhisattvas who serve as guardians of the True Dharma; they shall ensure that this great teaching is respectfully proclaimed."
At that time, there were sixty billion bodhisattvas in the assembly who, desiring to protect the true Dharma, rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, Great Sage!"

We shall all together receive this chapter on the Great Assembly of the Dharma from this sutra and disseminate it at all times throughout the ten directions and this Sahā world, so that all may receive its grace. Under the protective dharma-kingly authority of Maitreya Bodhisattva, we shall widely proclaim the essentials of this sutra.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are bodhisattvas who, in this degenerate age of the five turbidities, hear this sutra, uphold it, recite it, and read it, you should know that they have been established by Maitreya.
At that time, the Buddha praised the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O assembly of true beings!"

"If you, before the Buddha, exclaim your own resolve to protect the True Dharma, then you shall be protecting the True Dharma of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the rivers of the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, Great Sage!"
Please grant me your original forgiveness.

Regarding the scriptures I have recited, my strength was slight and my wisdom shallow; thus, the phrases and meanings I proclaimed may not have been complete. Therefore, I take refuge in the Buddha to absolve me of these transgressions, and I pay homage to all Bodhisattvas who uphold the inexhaustible Dharma.
The Buddha told Acchamata:
"The meanings of the Dharma phrases you have spoken follow one another in succession; not a single one deviates from principle, and you have attained unimpeded mastery.

If there is a bodhisattva who is free from the hindrances of the aggregates (skandha-nīvaraṇa), the teachings they proclaim will be without deficiency or omission, and their discernment of the meaning of the sutras will be exactly as they have stated."
How much more so now for this true sage, who expounds this sūtra with complete mastery of both its inner and outer meanings; how could his boundless deliverance not reach [all beings]?

Now, Akṣayamati has attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eloquence and wisdom he expounds are sovereign; yet, regarding the Mahāyāna, he has no need for external reliance or support, walking alone without peer, proclaiming the resolution of all doubts and ferrying others to the other shore.

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this stage of the path, their body, speech, and mind will never be deficient or leaking; they shall be the foremost in all wisdom, penetrating everything without exception, and their conduct of body, speech, and mind will be fully perfected.

The countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas of the ten directions all join in praising what you have expounded; now the Buddha’s own examination confirms that it is thorough in both its internal meaning and external expression, without a single omission, and the same is true for all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Thereupon Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the title of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This sutra is titled ‘The Inexhaustible Exposition of the Meanings, Principles, and Phrases by the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati,’ and its essential chapter is titled ‘The Chapter on Akṣayamati.’”

Ānanda! If there are those who receive this Dharma of the sutra, their minds will become increasingly clear and they will possess a powerful capacity for understanding its principles. Their merit and virtue will increase a hundred-thousandfold, and by explaining it to others, they establish the work of a Buddha.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the Venerable Ānanda, the devas, nāgas, and spirits were all filled with joy; they bowed their heads in prostration and departed.
The Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra, Scroll Seven.
